for measures that are economically attractive to society; and for
technical potential, $128 billion.
You might ask, Madam Speaker, what are the benefits of making this investment. Saving Canadians $150 billion probably is not a bad idea on its own. What about the other great benefit? We heard the Minister of the Environment, and we have heard the Prime Minister saying they are going to do all these great things about global warming. Even from the most recent conferences the government has not even been able to adopt the suggestion that Canada reduce the amount of C02 we are producing by 20 per cent by the year 2005. Yet it can do more than that and save Canadians $150 billion.
If I were a government member I might say: "Why is the minister of energy withholding this report from me as a government member if it is going to save Canadians $150 billion? We are slashing unemployment insurance. We are clawing back pension and family allowance. We are gouging middle and low-income taxpayers. We are kicking the crap out of this province and that province. What is going on?" Well, try and get a government member to talk seriously about hydrogen technology. They say: "Hydrogen, you cannot drive a car on hydrogen". Of course you can. If you have a beaker of water, you have got energy to drive a car. And government members say: "Good grief, this is not possible".
We have allowed a very select group, not just in Canada but around the world, to get a stranglehold on a lot of people. Whether it is for industrial or residential fuel consumption or for motor vehicles or for aircraft, there are alternate fuels, hydrogen being the prime one.
Why are we not moving on hydrogen? It does not create carbon dioxide. It is not going to add to the greenhouse effect. It is not polluting. The only thing that comes out of the tail pipe of your car is water and oxygen. I have people in my constituency who have already converted their vehicles and now they have all kinds of heat and pressure from the provincial government saying: "You are not taxes". There are intelligent approaches to be made.
The plea that I make to this chamber is that we start to use even a small fraction of the native intelligence that each of us was endowed with and the capacity to read. Why is a report that would save Canada $150 billion
Private Members' Business
being hidden in the safe in the minister of energy's office? Why will he not tell the Prime Minister? Why does he not come in here and say: "Look, I can save $150 billion. I can reduce the carbon dioxide being released into the atmosphere." We can do something serious. There are entire countries that are going to disappear between the oceans within the lifetime of many of the people sitting in this chamber if we do not do something about the greenhouse effect.
In conclusion, I could go on, as you could imagine, Madam Speaker, at some length about the benefits and the reasons why, not only members of Parliament but Canadians generally have a right to access environmental information that is vital to them in their community, to them and their family, to us as a global species and to the other species on the planet. We have paid for it as Canadians. We deserve access to that information, and I would hope that all members would support such a proposal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by saying that the government and, I am sure, all members of Parliament understand the importance of providing the public with the type of information which it needs in order to become informed and to build upon the concern which is already there with respect to manners in which we can collectively work together to improve the health of our environment.
Even a passing interest in public affairs and environmental issues would cause any observer in these last few months to understand and to appreciate the fact that there is a growing awareness of the importance of the environment. In a very real sense there is a thirst for knowledge and how we as individuals can lead toward that healthy environment.
I use as an example a letter I received from a constituent that really struck home. This constituent living in one of the smaller communities within Brandon-Souris wrote to say that she was heating her house with fuel oil. She wondered if in so doing she was contributing in any significant way to the degradation of the environment. I was pleased to use that particular example to go to the department to ask for the type of information she obviously wished to have in order for her

November 20, 1989
Private Members' Business
to determine whether or not she was doing her part to assist in the development of a healthy environment.
This is but one example of the importance of providing information to Canadians wherever they may live in such a way that it is comprehensible to them and that it meets their everyday need for knowledge.
I think it is also important that the information be as comprehensible and readily available as possible, because I sense there is a tremendous danger as well that sometimes a little information or information improperly understood can contribute to misinformation and sometimes unnecessary fears.
The whole area of the threat to the environment is so scientific in nature that many Canadians are having difficulty grappling with the information before them. I would hope and believe that the government is beginning to provide its information in such a way that it is, cohesive in nature and leads to the kind of better understanding which will permit Canadians as individuals to lead a healthier and more environmentally pleasing lifestyle, as well as enable them as individuals to play a role in policy making. There is no question that virtually everyone who is a part of public life in Canada today would concede the fact that the public in many instances is leading and government is at best responding. As a member of government, I would readily concede that. I must say to my hon. friend who has just spoken that I very much respect his knowledge of the environment. I readily recognize that his commitment to the issues has made him a leader in this House and throughout the nation. I would say, however, in defence of this government that I do believe it has done more than he has given it credit for in terms of trying to provide the kind of information the public is seeking. I refer specifically to the hearings which are taking place in Alberta with respect to proposed pulp mills there because the hon. member made reference to it.
I think most people who have followed those hearings would concede that the information provided by those who have spoken on behalf of the federal government has been information in depth. It has been information that has made a valuable contribution, although one cannot judge that process until it is completed.
I would say in passing that I think many people were surprised by the breadth of evidence made available to that hearing by the spokesmen on behalf of the Government of Canada. I would not like members of this House or the listening public in any way to fail to appreciate the extent of the knowledge being provided in the hearings and as part of the environmental assessment review process.
We have been doing one thing which I think is worth noting, that is, the development of a state of the environment reporting system. This system, as you know, is given legal recognition in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act under section 2 which states: "The government of Canada shall provide information to the people of Canada on the state of the Canadian environment."
As part of that process there has been created a public advisory committee to determine the type of information needed as part of state of the environment reporting and to ensure that the information provided is accurate, up to date, and meets the needs of Canadians wherever they may be. This committee consists of individuals from environmental groups, consumer organizations, industry and the academic community, all of which have a direct interest in the state of the environment and all of which recognize the importance of the dissemination of accurate and up to date information.
The government has made a very deliberate and, I think most members would agree, positive step to involve the community at large in the issues which are ours. The environmental issue is not something which is in any way unique to this House. In fact, one would be less than honest if one were to try and pretend for a moment that the House has led in the development of environmental issues throughout Canada because I do not think it has. I think it is following. I think it is providing equal leadership on occasion, but it has not in the strictest sense of the word led.
This government is trying to involve the public in ensuring that our knowledge is as complete as it can be and the information which we are providing is as comprehensive as it can be. One of the ways we are doing that is by involving as many people from all sectors of the community as we can.
In 1986 the first national state of the environment report was published. Following the example of other governments and other countries, a 260-page publication was issued examining conditions, trends and our renew-
November 20, 1989

able resource systems. It looked at the effects of our human activity on our ecosystems and discussed the responses of institutions and organizations to environmental change. We are now working on that second national report which is scheduled to be published in 1991.
In addition, the state of environment fact sheet series is made available. It is designed to stimulate interest in environmental concerns among the media, non-govem-mental groups, high school students, libraries and the interested public.
If I may say so in passing, I think one of the most encouraging things I have noticed these last few months is a very evident interest among young people in environmental issues and also their willingness to do the type of research they must do in order to be well informed. I think the state of the environment fact sheet series contributes to that. Also young people in the province of Ontario, by way of their own leadership, have contributed to changing practices in requiring fast food restaurants to provide the product to them in a more environmentally satisfying manner than had been the case before.
Young people, as a result of the kind of information which they have been accumulating, some of which has been provided by this government, some by other governments, and some by their own research, are now playing a positive role in the sense that they are going into the industry, exercising their power as consumers and demanding that product be provided to them in a way which is environmentally sound. At first their efforts to ensure that hamburger packages did not contain CFCs were scoffed at and management paid little attention to them. More recently I have noticed, however, that they have succeeded and now the products they wish to buy are being packaged in such a way that it is much more satisfying to them and much more environmentally safe than would otherwise be the case.
In addition to the fact sheet series which I mentioned before, there is the state of the environment report series which will feature insights into a wide variety of environmental issues of national and regional significance. These reports will be aimed at universities, resource managers and interest groups as well as at individuals who want information in depth. Some of
Private Members' Business
these reports currently under way deal with endangered species, peoples and parks, air quality, ground water, prairie water resources and impacts of global change.
In addition there is also the state of the environment reporting newsletter which we have made available three times a year. We are trying to build up a data base within Statistics Canada that will provide Canadians with quick access to a wide range of environmental information. Preliminary efforts have been made to develop key indicators of the state of the environment comparable to traditional economic indicators such as the Consumer Price Index. The availability of all this data will ensure that the public will have a greater access to information in the future than it had two, three or four years ago.
I think that all of us will benefit from that because a well informed public is certainly the most important step in ensuring the legislation and practices in this country and in other countries throughout the world are what they might be.
For too long, economic development has occurred at the expense of the natural and cultural environment. That, of course, was recognized and dramatized by the report associated with former Prime Minister Brund-tland and those who worked with her. One of the results of that, of course, is a growing interest in the words "sustainable development". It may well be that many Canadians as yet could not define the term "sustainable development", and if they were to attempt to, they probably would not agree on what that definition should be.
I think what has developed is a realization that Canadians, by acting together in as well informed a manner as possible and by ensuring that their governments act on their behalf as well that we can indeed ensure that economic development in the future will occur in such a way that it will not be at the expense of future generations as has occurred in the past. Unfortunately, in the past, we made decisions based almost entirely on economic considerations alone and later we asked what the environmental consequences of those decisions would be.
I think as a result of the information which is now being made available by government and others to the public, we will ensure that in the future, consideration of

November 20, 1989
Private Members' Business
the economic implications of a decision will be a forethought rather than an afterthought.

Madam Speaker, it seems to me that if the parliamentary secretary had read the commitments to open government made by his leader in the 1984 election and had been consistent with that pledge, he would also have had something positive to say in support of the motion of the member for Skeena and would have indicated his government's intention to let this motion pass. The Parliamentary Secretary refrained from saying that, however, ignoring the commitment of his own party to a more open government which was one of the basic pledges made in the summer of 1984.
Worse than that, the parliamentary secretary decided to develop a reply on the subject of transfer of general information and interpreted the motion of the member from Skeena as meaning that all he wants is to provide fact sheets, state of the environment reports and that kind of general information which we all know has been made available to the public but really contain very little hard data.
The member for Skeena talks with his motion about ensuring that all Canadians have right of access to all environmental information. He means the hard facts and the hard studies and the interesting stuff which does not see the light of day, if I understand his motion correctly. Of course there is merit in what he is proposing. The public ought to know about the hard econometric studies as to what are the options and policies when you make a decision affecting the economy, energy and other aspects that have an impact on the environment.
It would be a question, therefore, of making available to the public studies made on the cost of inaction on environmental matters or studies that I am sure are being made by the Department of the Environment on the evaluation of water quality in the Great Lakes about which we would like to know. What is the pattern and what do scientists in the employ of government say these days on this subject matter which is, however, not disclosed to the public on a matter that is basically one of public health.
The member would like, I am sure, to see studies made on energy options and the real cost of these energy options and he made a reference in his intervention to
that particular report which we would all dearly love to read. I am sure the public would like to know more.
Since I see the Minister of Labour in the House tonight, I will say that the public would like to know what studies are being conducted on the subject of ergonomics, on the subject of health at work, on the use of video screens and how that impacts on the health of workers. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to speak to a very important subject, namely, the public's right of access to all information on environmental matters. Madam Speaker, we cannot expect opposition members to consider the fact that things have been changing for a number of years and that this kind of information is becoming increasingly available. There were many references in the course of this debate to the situation in western Canada. I am more familiar with what is happening in eastern Canada and especially in Quebec, where the Government of Quebec is to be commended for environmental legislation that is among the strictest and most effective in this country. For instance, Madam Speaker, as a private citizen, I asked the Government of Quebec a few weeks ago to give me some vital information about mine tailings which are a major source of pollution in my region, and I did so following announcements made by the Minister of the Environment in Charlottetown, together with his colleagues, the provincial environment ministers, when it was decided to earmark $200 million for decontamination of abandoned sites in this country. I asked for a list of these sites, which happen to be mine tailings, and a week later, I was given all the information on these sites which are a health and environmental hazard for my region. This is one example to show that when we ask for information about subjects that concern us, that information is available.

November 20, 1989
Private Members' Business
Madam Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to show that the situation has improved in the past few years, and that as far as the environment is concerned, the federal government is making more and more information available to Canadians.
The government is so aware of these issues that it now has a vast range of programs, provinding the public with access to up-to-date information on climatic change, water quality, land, forests and other natural resources in this country. The most recent and most exhaustive program is the system of reports on the status of the environment included in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act we passed in 1987, and I quote: "The federal government shall provide information to the people of Canada on the state of the Canadian environment".
Reports on the state of the environment are an excellent way of identifying problems and setting priorities, because after all, actions speak louder than words when the delicate balance of our planet is threatened.
Following the example of countries like the United States, Australia, France, Sweden and Japan, Canada in 1986 published its first national report on the state of the environment, a document of some 270 pages that looked at our use of renewable resources and our policies in this area, the impact of human activity on our ecosystems and the way our institutions and organizations respond to environmental changes. The second edition, which is to appear in 1991, will include information provided by federal agencies, the provinces and territories, and industrial, academic and non-governmental groups. I am convinced that from such a diverse report will come a complete and accurate description of the state of the environment in Canada, in a form that is easily accessible to the public.
In order to add to knowledge on the state of the environment, the federal environment minister has begun to publish a series of information leaflets dealing with important environmental issues and trends and their impact on the natural world, economic opportunities, health and quality of life. These leaflets are intended to make the media, non-governmental organizations, high schools, libraries and the public more aware of environmental concerns.
This series of leaflets was launched last year with the publication of The Urbanization of Rural Canada, 1981-86, which dealt with the loss of agricultural and other resource-rich land as it was converted to urban use. This publication of the Canadian Wildlife Service reports on the urbanization of rural land in 70 regions of Canada. Coming leaflets will deal with the contamination of sea birds and the pollution of the marine environment in British Columbia, among other subjects.
The department also intends to better inform the public by publishing complementary reports on the state of the environment which will shed light on a host of national or regional environmental issues. These reports will be for universities, resource managers and interest groups, as well as anyone who wants detailed information on specific subjects. Reports are now being prepared, in particular, on endangered species, the public, parks, air quality, ground water, water resources in the Prairies and the impact of change on a global scale.
Madam Speaker, we also want to encourage exchanges of information between governments, individuals and non-governmental organizations interested in approaches, methods and publications in connection with reports on the state of the environment; to this end, we will publish a state of the environment bulletin three times a year. At Statistics Canada we are also setting up a data bank which will give everyone instant access to a wide range of environmental information. Preliminary efforts have been made to define key environmental indicators similar to economic indicators such as the consumer price index. This source of information will prove invaluable useful to Canadians who want to know how to improve the environment.
Now more than ever, Madam Speaker, Canadians are deeply concerned about environmental problems. They have also expressed their willingness to share responsibilities for their future on this planet. That is why, if we hope to preserve and improve global environment, Environment Canada must let people know about environmental changes and their consequences. For too long now economic development has been pursued at the expense of the natural and cultural environment. The World Commission on Environment and Development, chaired by Mrs. Gro Brundtland, called for a reversal of this tendency in favor of sustainable development. Every
November 20, 1989

Canadian will have a key role to play in the achievement of this objective.
By giving people the means of information they need to shape their destiny, we believe they will be in a better position to exert an influence on the health of the environment. Environmental reports give us a better perspective on ourselves and our habitat. They are the foundation of sound resource planning and management. We hope that the people will put this information to good use. The success of environmental reports depends on everyone taking part in the protection of our environment.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member's concern for the well-being of our environment is shared by millions of Canadians. I am sure that he would agree that the protection of our natural resources is a serious responsibility and one that requires the legislative power to prosecute polluters as well as to protect the rights of individuals who have provided Environment Canada with confidential information for the good of the country.
Without legislation governing the disclosure of information to the public, our ability to protect every Canadian's right to a healthy environment would be seriously impeded. Under existing legislation, exemptions from disclosure relating to environmental issues, as well as other information within the federal government, are specified in the Access to Information Act.
If I may quote from Section 20(1) of the Act:
The head of a government institution shall refuse to disclose any record requested under this Act that contains:
(a) trade secrets of a third party; (b) financial, commercial, scientific or technical information that is confidential information supplied to a government institution by a third party and is treated consistently in a confidential manner by the third party; (c) information the disclosure of which could reasonably be expected to result in material financial loss or gain to, or could reasonably be expected to result in material financial loss or gain to, or could reasonably be expected to prejudice the competitive position of a third party; or (d) information the disclosure of which could reasonably be expected to interfere with contractual or other negotiations of a third party.
To summarize, these exemptions are generally designed to protect information that has been submitted to
Private Members' Business
the government on a confidential basis. Environment Canada receives much information through confidential consultations and negotiations with provinces as well as with other countries. The total release of this information would seriously damage the department's ability to carry on these relationships and would hamper our negotiating position.
It should also be noted that the department and the Conservation and Protection Service, in particular, gathers information in the course of investigations that may lead to prosecutions against polluters. If this information were to be released without agreement by the third party involved, as specified in the Access to Information Act, it could well compromise the success of any subsequent investigation.
As well, the consequences of releasing trade secrets and other confidential business information under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act should be selfevident. Sources could be reluctant to divulge important information for fear that public disclosure could prejudice their competitive position in the market or result in material financial loss.
There is already an extremely thorough public interest provision for disclosure in Section 20(6) of the Access to Information Act. It states:
The head of a government institution may disclose any record requested under this Act, or any part thereof, that contains information described in paragraph (1) (b), (c) or (d) if that disclosure would be in the public interest as it relates to public health, public safety or protection of the environment and, if the public interest in disclosure clearly outweighs in importance any financial loss or gain to, prejudice to the competitive position of or interference with contractual or other negotiations of a third party.
In addition, other legislation, particularly the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, CEPA, has provisions dealing with access to environmental information, including the possibility of public interest disclosure. CEPA limits the type of information that can be considered confidential and allows for a number of circumstances in which information may be disclosed.
Section 20(2) of CEPA specifies the wide range of types of information that may be disclosed. These include information on a substance's use, its safe handling, its disposal and elimination, safety measures to be taken in case of accidents involving a substance, certain physical and chemical data on a substance, a substance's effect on health, safety and the ecology and the methods and

November 20, 1989
Private Members' Business
results of product or environmental tests done on a substance by or for a government institution.
Section 20(4) of CEPA indicates various circumstances in which information may be disclosed, namely:
(a) with the written consent of the person who provided it or on whose behalf it was provided; (b) as may be necessary for the purposes of this Act; (c) under an agreement between the Government of Canada and the government of a province or of a foreign country, or between the Minister and any other Minister of the Crown in right of Canada where (i) the purpose of the agreement is the administration or enforcement of any law, and (ii) the government of the province or foreign country or the other Minister undertakes to keep the information confidential; (d) to a physician or prescribed medical professional who requests the information for the purpose of making a medical diagnosis of, or rendering medical treatment to, a person in an emergency; or (e) in accordance with the Access to Information Act.
Further, Section 20(6) of CEPA specifies circumstances under which the Minister may disclose information on 24-hour notice. I will quote from this section:
Notwithstanding subsection (3), the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act, the Minister may disclose information-where (a) the disclosure is in the interest of public health, public safety or the protection of the environment; and (b) the public interest in the disclosure clearly outweighs the importance of any material financial loss or prejudice to the competitive position of the person who provided the information or on whose behalf it was provided.
Clearly, the implications of removing all restrictions on the access to information regarding the environment would not serve the interests of Canadians in situations where it could seriously hamper the government's abilities to protect the right to a healthy environment.
I ask the hon. member to consider seriously the negative implications that such a change would have on the government's ability to collect information that is vital to the protection of the environment.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-28, an act to amend the Income Tax Act, the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, the Old Age Security Act, the Public Utilities Income Ihx Transfer Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act and a related Act be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, I rise today on behalf of senior citizens in my riding to debate the legislation before the House.
Bill C-28 will, in effect, put an end to Canada's most respected and envied social programs. In fact, the Canadian Seniors Network described the measures in the April budget more precisely. In its summer newsletter One Voice this organization said, "History will remember the clawback as the end of universality, not for its drop in the deficit bucket."
Senior citizens in Kenora-Rainy River have never been more disillusioned than with this Conservative government. This is not the government's first attempt to destroy universal social programs. In 1985, the Conservative government tried to deindex old age pensions even after the Prime Minister had solemnly pledged during the 1984 election campaign that, "social programs were a sacred trust never to be tampered with."
Senior citizens in this country believed the Prime Minister in 1984 but they soon realized how wrong they had been. The government will say it listened to the voice of senior citizens in 1985 and withdrew the deindexing proposal. In reality, the government backed down in the face of a public outcry by seniors right across Canada.
The Prime Minister continued to assure senior citizens since the 1985 coup attempt on old age pensions that his government would preserve and protect social programs. During the 1988 general election the Prime Minister,
Government Orders
standing on the stage with his own mother, repeated his pledge.
Senior citizens in Kenora-Rainy River no longer believe anything this government says. They know that as soon as one promise is made, another is broken. My constituents know that this Conservative government has a hidden agenda when it comes to universal programs. One of the government's own members admitted as much in an article which appeared in The Ottawa Citizen on September 23. The chairman of the House of Commons finance committee said that his government's real agenda was to do away with universal social programs.
The clawback provisions for old age security benefits and family allowances are a definite and real threat to Canada's social programs. There is widespread opposition to the clawback measure. The government says that everyone must help to reduce the deficit. Many respected Canadians and senior organizations say otherwise.
Allow me to quote from a few sources. Don MacGilli-vray said in The Ottawa Citizen September 14, "The policy pretends to continue universality but in fact cancels it."
Hugh Winsor of The Globe and Mail said on May 5, "If, as Mr. Mulroney subsequently admitted, tampering with the indexation was wrong in 1985, attempting the same thing with the threshold levels is wrong in 1989.
Leonard Shifrin said in an article published in The Ottawa Citizen on May 4 that the finance minister proceeded to undermine the universality of family allowances and old age pensions.
A report from the National Council of Welfare states, "A social program that delivers benefits to everyone and then collects them all back from some recipients is not universal."
The President of the Canadian Council of Retirees, Bill Corns, said in a Toronto Star interview on May 7, "This is the start of the end of universality and an introduction of a means test."
So there you have it. Everyone who looks at the clawback provisions believes that this government is putting an end to universal social programs. If the clawback provision goes through, what is there to stop this government from attacking other universal programs? We have already seen changes to the unemploy-

November 20, 1989
Government Orders
ment insurance system which threatens universality. What's next? Medicare? Canada Pension? Who knows?
Within 10 years close to one million Canadian families who currently receive family allowances or old age security pensions will begin to lose their benefits due to the partial indexing of the 50 per cent threshold. It is estimated that by the year 2000 the threshold will fall to the equivalent of $35,000 in today's dollars. By the time the baby boom generation reaches retirement most will have to repay their benefits under the clawback provision.
Furthermore, once Canadians accept the principle of the clawback provision as part of our system, there is nothing to stop the government from setting the threshold as it sees fit.
Canadians do not support the clawback provision and they will never accept it. Canadians are prepared to share the burden of deficit reduction. Flowever, they are not prepared to carry the burden alone.
My constituents want to see responsible government spending. They do not tolerate the millions of dollars spent to promote the goods and services tax. My constituents believe, as I do, that universal social programs are a right of citizenship. As the Right Elon. Leader of the Opposition stated to this House on October 11, it is part of the social contract in return for a lifetime of contribution to our community.
Reducing the deficit on the backs of senior citizens is unfair and it is downright criminal. I myself have a large seniors population in my riding, senior citizens make up 18 per cent of the population of Kenora-Rainy River. I have been inundated with calls and letters opposing this measure. Senior citizens are telling me that they are living in fear for their future. They see their incomes reduced as a result of higher taxes. Not only is the government taking away what they have spent their lives working for, it is imposing a 9 per cent tax on goods and services. Senior citizens are having to live on a tighter budget because of reduced buying power.
Senior citizens in Kenora-Rainy River are worried that further erosion of their benefits and increased taxes will mean that the rest of their lives will be spent in
poverty. Many of them remember the depression years and wonder if they will have to relive that time in 1989.
The clawback provision is also extremely discriminatory. It attacks one income families like no other measure. A family with two incomes, each earning less than $50,000 will not have to repay any family allowance benefits. However, a single income family with two children earning $56,000 a year will see its family allowance benefits clawed back. Where is the fairness in this? I think the clawback provision will have the most devastating effect on single parent families earning over $50,000 per year. That sounds like a lot of money but when you have children and are on your own, I do not think that is a whole lot of money in today's world. There are more expenses in a single parent family than in a two parent families.
I was speaking with a constituent of mine over the weekend who is a single parent with two children. One child is in grade two and the other child is a preschooler. My constituent has a net income of $54,000 per year. That sounds like a lot of money. Her job requires that she attend meetings in the evening and on occasion she must travel on weekends. My constituent pays for child care services during the day for her preschooler and babysitting fees in addition for her grade two child after school. On top of that she must pay additional babysitting fees in the evenings when she has meetings and on weekends when she must travel. She is faced with higher transportation costs as a result of driving her children around.
Given that she is a single parent, she must also take time off work when there are functions at the school or when her children are sick. The family allowance benefits she receives every month have helped her to defray some of these costs. They at least cover some of the gas expenses for her car. Why should she have her benefits clawed back? She is already paying taxes on the family allowance benefits she receives through the income tax system. My constituents looks at the clawback provision and she worries about her family's future.
She has worked extremely hard to provide her young children with a good family life. She is dedicated to providing her family with a secure future. Why should my constituent be discriminated against because she is a
November 20, 1989

single parent? Why should she be penalized for working hard at providing her children with a financially secure environment?
The goods and services tax will further erode her income. She told me that the clawback of her family allowance benefits, combined with the goods and services tax and higher personal income taxes, will mean a net reduction of some 6 per cent in her income. She does not see these measures as a fair distribution of the burden, nor.do we on this side of the House. These measures discriminate against seniors and against families.
The government must withdraw the clawback provisions of old age security benefits and family allowances. Our Canadian senior citizens and families must be treated equally and fairly. The universality of our social programs must be preserved as a sacred trust. I ask the members opposite to consider that before they put this very discriminatory legislation into law.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to participate in tonight's marathon session. I was assuming I was going to start nine minutes from now but my neighbour to the west surprised me.
I want to start by reflecting on events that led up to all of us being here. As I look at the clock I think back to what I was doing this time 365 days ago. I was in the final poll on election night working to pull out the voters to make sure their votes counted, getting them to the ballot box. I say that in terms of reflecting on why we are here tonight under the imposition of closure, why we are debating a piece of legislation that we believe fundamentally changes this country and the manner in which it is operated.
I want to take you back in time to March 7, 1984 when the then-to-be Prime Minister said, and this was recorded in a CP wire story, "Our position is simple and straightforward. We are in favour of universality of social programs and it shall not be touched."
Then after four years of majority government, on the election trail once again the Prime Minister, in Summer-side, an interesting location in which to make pronouncement about the future, told senior citizens this:
Government Orders
Let me say a special word to the senior citizens. In the future Canada will be doing more, not less, for all of you. As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished, by our government which is committed to social justice and fairness to Canadians.
Here we are a year to the date of the eve of the election. A year ago at eight o'clock the polls closed, returned the Conservatives with less of a majority, but a majority albeit. And what has happened to the promises? Tonight is a prime example. We are debating a bill that eliminates universality for our old age pensions and for our family allowances. How does it do that? It does it by clawing back those universal benefits at a certain threshold; in terms of the old age security at $50,000.
You may ask what is wrong with that. Two things. First of all, the whole point of universality is the minimization of the bureaucracy required to administer such a scheme. It means that every Canadian who reaches that magic age qualifies. It is much easier, much more efficient, and much more cost effective, dare I use that phrase, to have everybody on the list rather than establishing some sort of means test, whether it is tied into the income tax system or through specific applications or what have you. It is much more efficient in terms of the cost of delivering that service.
I do not have the figures with me, but I can give you the ranges of an answer to an order paper question provided to me by the Conservative government in, I believe, 1985 or 1986. I asked what was the cost of delivering those income support programs. I was amazed to find that the most efficient income support program, the cheapest per hundred dollars to get a hundred dollar cheque into the hands of a Canadian citizen, was old age security, including the income supplement. It was down around 32 cents per $100. Family allowance was not too far away from that. But then we get into the real heavy ones, the ones that this government likes to attack, such as unemployment insurance, with all of its checks and balances. It was up around $8 or $9 per $100 to deliver.
When I checked with the local welfare officials of the city of Thunder Bay, it was $13 per $100 to deliver that service. Workers Compensation in Ontario was around $18.
Just from the aspect of efficiency, let alone the humanity involved, it makes much more sense to have a universal program than one that is selective.

November 20, 1989
There is another reason, and that is why we pride ourselves as a nation on treating all of our people, as much as possible, in the same way. By providing every senior with the full benefit of his or her pension, or every family with the full benefit of the family allowance, we are making a statement to the world. We are saying that we care about our citizens. We as a society are prepared to assist those who have less than we do. That is extremely important. It is also important that we recognize the value of those programs. Yes, there are people, both seniors and families who "don't need the extra money".
Old age security and family allowance are already part of the income tax system. If you make more money, you pay more money back into the system, and that is only fair. So what is happening to seniors in this case, in terms of the clawback, is double taxation. The same thing for families. It is not as if they are getting a free ride. It is not as if they are getting the full benefit of the income support. They are paying their fair share based on their ability to pay. That is the way it should be.
Let us go back to the promises made by this government time and time again. Before the election, government members used words like "sacred trust" and "supportive universality", all those very nice phrases that brought warmth to the heart. They were all lies. There was clearly no intention whatsoever of fulfilling them. The Minister of Finance, a few days before the election a year ago, said that all our promises are spending commitments. We have money to pay for it. Lo and behold, all of a sudden we do not have any money to pay for then. We do not have money for VIA Rail. Where is the child care program that was promised for the day after they got re-elected? We will bring in a child care program, they said.
Well, it is a year and no child care program. That is the kind of government we have in power in Canada these days, a government that has no qualms whatsoever of saying one thing to people before the election and not only just not doing it after the election, but doing the opposite. The attack on universality, the attack on VIA Rail, the lack of child care policies, the attack on unemployment insurance, the attack on post-secondary education, where again the Prime Minister promised
Government Orders
that we would do better than ever before. What do we find? We find cuts, reductions of transfer payments to the provinces that can least afford to lose the money.
Perhaps it is okay for me to be from Ontario and say, "We're okay. We can afford it." But in some of the prairie provinces, and specifically the Atlantic provinces, the only hope is the human resource and access to higher education so that they can go on to build a better life for all of us. But no, this government is cutting funding in that area as well.
That is not why the Conservatives were elected to govern this country. People believed them when they said they had enough money to live up to their commitments, that the deficit was no longer a problem, that they had it managed, it was under control. I have to wonder how it can be under control on the eve of November 20, 1988, and then two days later, after the dust settles, it is chaos, it is a major crisis, that we need to reconsider everything that we have committed ourselves to. They never did use the word "promise", maybe because people have a great suspicion about promises. Maybe they do not think that promises will be kept. But when the finance minister, supported by the Prime Minister, says that these are commitments, we have the money in the bank to pay for these, people say, "Maybe this time they are going to live up to it, maybe they really mean what they say".
We have seen over the last year that there was never any intention to live up to those commitments, that this government had a very specific agenda. As the current Minister for International Trade once said, "If we told you what we were going to do, you would never elect us, you would never vote for us". For all of his failings, the hon. minister is a very honest man. He tells it like it is. When we said, "Look what he is saying, you had better listen to him", people said, "Oh, no, no, no, he doesn't know what he is talking about." The government said, "No, he doesn't know what he is talking about. We are going to live up to our commitments".
The commitments have not been lived up to. The people of Canada have been sold out. They gave their vote to a particular party but were really robbed of it because they expected something in exchange. They certainly did not get what they expected. That is very unfortunate because that taints all of us.
November 20, 1989

In this House we are partisans. Whether it is between the Conservatives and the New Democrats or the New Democrats and the Liberals, we pick at each other because that is the nature of our parliamentary system. But those kind of lies fundamentally undermine the political parties and the system in this country because people will look at us and say, "Well, if we can't trust them how are we going to trust you folks? What makes you say that you will be any different?" My answer of course is, "Try us, and if you don't like us then you can boot us out too", which I hope the people of Canada will do to the hon. members opposite. It seems that the government cannot be straightforward with the people of Canada and this really bothers me.
Let me return for about five minutes, if my clock reads correctly-as you know, Madam Speaker, I have had some disputes with the clock in this House over time, but never in terms of five-minute spans and not with you but with one of the gentlemen who sits in that chair, has knees like mine, but was able to play football a lot better than I was.
In terms of the clawback itself, the Minister of Finance says it will have a minimal effect on Canadian individuals and families. He may believe that. For example, he claims that only 4.3 per cent of seniors will be paying back part or all of their pensions, with 54,000 individuals paying back all of their OAS and 74,000 paying back a part of it. On family allowances, he claims that only 14 per cent of families will be affected; 368,000 of them mind you, paying back all of their family allowance and
167,000	paying back a part of it.
The important thing to note, though, is that that is for this year. That figure is going to go up rapidly year by year so that more and more retirees will end up repayng their pensions and more and more famlies will repay all of their family allowances.
Here is how it works. The income level at which the clawback starts will move upwards according to the same deindexing formula that exists in the tax system, i.e., inflation minus 3 per cent. This means that if you assume an inflation rate of 4.5 per cent, which I think is about where we are at right now, the income limit will move up by only 1.5 per cent a year. A worker earning $40,000 a
Government Orders
year and watching his or her income rise with inflation will be earning enough to put his income over the clawback level for family allowances of $56,309 by 1997.
When we think about that, that still seems like a lot of money. But I can tell you that when I was earning $20,000 at Parks and Rec a number of years ago, having started at $6,000 a few years before, $20,000 was quite a significant sum of money. So we have to recognize what inflation does and what wage increases do over time. Ultimately, hundreds of thousands of people will be affected by the clawback. People who are working now expecting to retire in 25 years will be included and they will have a healthy level of income according to 1989 dollars but it will be eaten away so that more and more Canadians will be caught by this big claw.
It will come to a point where more people will not get it than people who will get it. That is one of the other reasons why we fundamentally oppose the concept of the clawback, because of its impact on the social services program, the income support programs of this country.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank you for giving me the opportunity to join the debate on Bill C-28.
Still, Madam Speaker, I can hardly say I am pleased to take part in a debate on a legislative measure which strikes at the basic principle of the universality of Canada's social programs.
Besides, the government is going after elderly people and families when it launches such an attack against old age pensions and family allowances. Only a callous government would so mistreat seniors and Canadian families.
Madam Speaker, you will certainly ask me how the government goes about attacking all these people. Well, let me explain. This bill includes 59 amendments to the Income Tax Act, 59 amendments which signal the demise of social programs of which Canadians are so proud.
The principle of universality was adopted so that all Canadians would be treated the same way and to create such a feeling of belonging to the community as would make it possible for all Canadians to share the riches of their country and be entitled to certain benefits.
This Bill marks the end of all that. No more universality, no more social justice, no more equity in Canada. This is the beginning of the end for this government.
Yes, Madam Speaker, the beginning of the end for this government which in 1986 began to levy a special income surtax which it described as being temporary. Well, surtaxes are still with us. They went up, from 3 to 5 per cent. Talk about nerve, Madam Speaker.
As to the family allowances and old age pensions clawback provisions contained in this bill, they only confirm the fact that the government has gone too far and driven one more nail into its own coffin. The Prime Minister told us in 1984 that social programs were a sacred trust which was untouchable. He repeated the same thing in 1988. Now this legislative measure tells us that the Prime Minister did not keep his word and that he is heartless. The Prime Minister and his heartless
government have given us umpteen examples of their insensitivity towards Canadians. They once assured us that VIA Rail passenger transport services were extremely important and that they would be maintained at any cost. Yet not so long ago we learned that VIA services would be cut by one half.
Madam Speaker, the government's unemployment insurance reform is a sure sign of its insensitivity: henceforth Canadian workers will simply have to accept shorter benefit periods and pay for training programs.
Canadians in a number of communities will also have to accept the fact that they no longer have access to their own post offices.
Madam Speaker, the new tax on goods and services, the deplorable condition of infrastructures throughout the country, the reduction of funds earmarked for regional development-I will not mention them all-are as many concrete examples of the heartlessness of this government.
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister told us on many occasions that social programs were a sacred trust, but what he says and what he does are two different things.
The obvious danger when one begins to tamper with the principle of universality of social programs is that the whole thing hangs in the balance. When they reduce the rates to the minimum, they give themselves the power to reduce them even further. Then it becomes difficult to know who is entitled to benefits, where to draw the line, and who will be in a position to decide which of our fellow citizens most need assistance.

Bill C-28 shows us that the government does not care about seniors. It does not care about Canada's social net. It does not care about the needs of the regions and it does not care about students. This bill puts an end to universality.
The National Council of Welfare in the annual report which it tabled last month claimed that this clawback puts an end to universality. It strongly urged the government to abandon its clawback proposals.
The National Council of Welfare is a citizens' advisory group appointed by cabinet to advise the government on
November 20, 1989

matters of social policy. The council's annual report strongly decries the government for its harsh policies.
This National Council of Welfare has claimed that the move away from universal benefits is the most significant change in social policy in a generation and that the Minister of Finance announced this change in the last budget speech with no prior consultation.
The Council further reported that the federal government had publicly rejected the idea of a clawback or surtax on old age pensions as late as January 1985 on the grounds that it would seriously disrupt the retirement income system. The government is now changing the rules of the game without obtaining the consent of Canadian seniors. Does the government not understand that these people have already paid for their old age pensions through a lifetime of hard work and paying taxes?
In the case of family allowances, the National Council of Welfare made it very clear when it said that the clawback discriminates against one-earner families because it is based on individual net income. For instance, a one-earner family with two children and a net income of $56,000 would lose all its family allowance benefits. On the other hand, a family with two incomes where one spouse earns $45,000 and the other $35,000 would escape the clawback despite the fact that they are making a total of $80,000.
Is that what you would call fair? Is that what Canadians have come to expect from their government? Will the rich keep getting richer and the poor sink further and further below the poverty line? As long as this government is in power, the answer is clear. This is a government that does not care for this country and its traditions. It is deliberately undermining the social fabric of the Canadian federation. How much longer will families and seniors have to put up with this type of government?
The National Council of Welfare does not stand alone in its criticism of this legislation. The Senior Citizens' Federation has also claimed that the clawback is biased, grossly inequitable and that it seriously undermines the principle of universality.
In a letter to the Prime Minister, the President of the Seniors' Federation, Mr. Les Batterson said with respect to this policy: "We view this proposal as a serious breach
Government Orders
of faith by our government, an insidious effort to undercut the social security programs that you have on numerous occasions stated are a sacred trust".
Mr. Batterson also added later in his letter: "We are also aware that we had previous deficits as serious as the present one and the government of the day did not tax back pensions to which Canadians had every reason to believe they had the genuine right."
The present government has often claimed that the deficit imposes an unfair burden on future generations; that the deficit indeed is larger than what some economists believe. Indeed, it has cut many programs which were vital to the future of this country in its efforts to reduce this deficit. With this mean-spirited legislation, it is now taxing back the pension benefits of those who worked hard to build this country, and it is reducing family allowances, all in the name of reducing the deficit.
However, despite the Prime Minister's constant rhetoric about the need for budgetary restraint and the downsizing of government, Treasury Board estimates show that his own Privy Council Office budget will jump almost $5 million. It will go up to $59.1 million in the next fiscal year and its staff will increase from 579 to 591.
What is sauce for the goose should also be sauce for the gander. How can the Prime Minister preach budgetary restraint to everyone while increasing his own budget? Moreover, how can the Prime Minister justify attacking the families and seniors of this country in order to achieve his aims?
To all intents and purposes Bill C-28 spells the end for universality of social programs. The Canadian Council on Social Development has said that the government is eroding the fundamental principle of universality which requires the collective responsibility of caring for children and seniors. It is doing so by withdrawing family allowance benefits from approximately 368,000 families and by eliminating old age benefits from 54,000 seniors. Furthermore, it will be reducing the amount of these benefits for many other families and seniors.
What the Conservative government is doing to this country is unimaginable. Over the next five years the clawback of family allowances will withdraw $1.68 billion from family budgets. This means that $500 million a year will be withheld from these families. That is outrageous.

These families cannot afford this kind of loss or reduction in their incomes.
In conclusion, I would like to say that every organization representing families and seniors in this country has said that the government is eliminating universality. If the government had been really honest, it would during the last election campaign have told everyone that it would end universality, that it would gut VIA Rail and that it would cut unemployment insurance benefits. If this government had had the courage to clearly spell out its intentions before the Canadian people it would not be standing where it is today. The Canadian people would not have elected a government which knew that it would be bringing down these Draconian policies.
Finally, a government which claims that the deficit imposes an unfair burden on future generations should ask itself whether the imposition of substandard education and health services, dilapidated transportation and communication infrastructure which will inevitably result in this fixation with the deficit does not impose an unfair burden on future generations.

Madam Speaker, I rise with more than mixed feelings. The definition of "mixed feelings" is watching your banker go over a cliff in your new car.
I want to say that the basic principle of universality is that it is universal-there are no ifs, ands, or buts, no qualifications, no hestitations. There used to be measures in the Criminal Code, I do not know if they are still there or not, concerning perverts and perversion. If there ever was a perversion of the principle of universality, this is it. You cannot have it both ways. It is either universal and people get it as a matter of right or you snoop into all their private affairs, their incomes and so forth and withhold some or all of it because in the view of the government of the day, no matter what political stripe, that is more than they need or more than they should get.
There is a basic flat in all of this, and I will repeat myself, it is either universal or it is not. If the government wanted to be completely honest, it would say that universality should be scrapped or severely amended so that anyone getting more than so much does not get it or
not all of it. No, it does not have the courage of its convictions to do that.
All my working life I think I have tried hard to make my contribution to my country in the various occupations I have been in, on the railroad, working for my party, as a member of Parliament, working for some farmers, that sort of thing. I have paid my taxes. During the late 1940s, the 1950s and the 1960s, I believe even into the early 1970s, when you made out your income tax there was an item stating "Old Age Security Fund". I believe, certainly back in the 1950s and 1960s it was 3 per cent. It varied from around 2 per cent, 3 per cent or 4 per cent. I paid for the dam thing.
Madam Speaker, this is a confession. I am going to put in my application this month for my old age pension. I do not look like I should be doing it. I do not act like it. I did not know whether to laugh or cry when I was making out the application.
I spent all these years earning my old age security pension. It is not all that much. It might come to $4,000 a year. I am not sure. But I spent all my working life earning it, and my fellow Canadians who could not earn it were also entitled to it. My fellow Canadians who did not need it were entitled to it and got it because it was universal, pure and simple.
I will never forget a fellow that I fought against-and I fought against his party for a lot of years-Louis St. Laurent. At that time we had not reduced the retirement age to 65, it was at 70. Mr. St. Laurent was Prime Minister of Canada. He had a sort of semi-public ceremony at which the press were present to receive his first old age pension cheque to emphasize the universal principle of old age assistance pensions. Whether or not you needed it, it was universal.
I also will never forget when my honoured colleague, Stanley Knowles, reached the age of 65. That is a long time ago, but then I have been here a fair while. Arthur Laing from British Columbia was the Minister of Public Works. We had a party for Stanley downstairs in Room 112 North. Arthur presented him with his first old age security pension cheque. He guaranteed him that the Government of Canada, no matter of what political stripe, would ever consider that a conflict of interest- after all the years of fighting Stanley did for pensioners.
