Before I got the opportunity to speak in this debate, I made it a point to read the letter that Mackenzie King sent to J. S. Woodsworth in, I think it was, 1924 or 1926, somewhere in there. It was a minority Parliament. In the letter he guaranteed that the government would bring in the first old age pension and unemployment insurance. Reading Canadian history and listening to old timers in my party, there were only two of them left, Woodsworth and A. A. Heaps, Woodsworth got up and said: "Mr. Speaker, I welcome this. On behalf of my group we will support this measure." It was $20 a month at age 70 with a means test. A. A. Heaps got up and said: "Mr. Speaker,
I support my leader. He's the leader and I'm the group."
The long history of the efforts of people in this country enabled us to arrive at just where we are now, people of all political persuasions, of every kind of group you could think of in this nation. We finally got to it.
Let me give you an example, Madam Speaker. I refer to someone who gets a company pension after 25, 35, 45 or whatever number of years of work of, say, $45,000 or $50,000 a year to which they contributed tens of thousands of dollars, but had been allowed to deduct the contributions from their income tax. When they drew the pension, they would have to pay income tax on it. It was the same with the Canada Pension, which I think is a good deal. It could still use some improving, but it is a good deal, especially for the younger people.
If you add the two together you are looking at $52,000, $54,000 or $55,000 a year gross pension from employment pension and Canada Pension. I have done some calculating. A person in that category will pay somewhere between $15,000 and $17,000 income tax on those two pensions, plus a clawback of some or all of their old age pension.
I suppose people like us from the NDP are not noted for supporting the wealthy. I suspect we have some reputation, depending on your point of view whether it is good or bad. You pay on a basic, fundamental principle based on ability to pay. Nobody is complaining about what you will pay on your company pension or your Canada Pension. That is perfectly proper. But on something that is supposed to be universal, to tax back some
Government Orders
or all of it from people who, for all of their working lives, or even if they weren't working got it as a matter of fundamental right as a Canadian citizen, a basic right which has been established since the 1920s, brings me back to the whole question of perversion.
If someone is making $75,000, 100,000 or $1 million a year, I do not care what the amount, you get them to pay their share through some other way, but old age security and the family allowance are inviolable. I repeat, they are either universal or they are not. The government had better make up its mind and say: "We are no longer going to have universal pensions". I know there are some who say, both in this House and outside: "No use giving them the universal pensions, they do not need it". That immediately denies the principle of universality.
The other thing is something that is going to affect me and many hon. members of this House when we are no longer here, either because we get defeated or retire, but we will leave that aside. We cannot say that we are suffering. But for tens of thousands of people earning the amounts I mentioned earlier, they will be lucky if they net $30,000 a year. One is not going to live very high off the hog on that, not in this day and age. That is only about $6,000 or $7,000 above the poverty level. The government wants to start a clawback on old age pensions or family allowances when these people's net pay is around the $30,000 mark. This flies in the face of any kind of reason and decency. For my hon. friend who is sitting there and not paying attention, I want to say it even flies in the face of Christian decency.
The other thing that is scary and worrisome is this. What is to prevent this government or a succeeding government of the same or a different political stripe from saying: "Well, we think the $50,000 is too high, let us make it $40,000, and apply that to both the Old Age Security pension and family allowances"? What is to prevent any government, now or later, once the principle of universality is betrayed and perverted from saying: "Well, if your income is over a certain amount, then you have to pay half of your own hospital bills and doctor bills"? What is to prevent the government if your income is over $50,000, or whatever amount is set by the government of the day, from saying: "Your kid is going to university and your income is over that amount, you're

November 20, 1989
Government Orders
going to pay half, three-quarters or all of the cost of that university education"? This flies in the face of any kind of decent reasoning.
There are other ways for the government to recover more than what it loses in income taxes or clawbacks out of the old age pension. There are many ways to do it. I can make a few suggestions. We keep getting asked by the Minister of Finance: "What is your alternative?". How about a 10 per cent tax on deferred corporation taxes? That will bring in nearly $4 billion a year, and it is nearly four points below the current interest rate.
How about closing some loopholes in income tax, both for individuals and for corporations, which are totally out of date compared to when they were brought out? How about restoring the corporate tax rate to what it was in 1984? That is worth $4 billion to $5 billion a year. I have not noticed corporations passing their production and their goods on to us consumers at lower prices. All that has happened is that they kept the money. That is all that has happened.
I recall a famous occasion in the 1950s when the government of that day decided to take the 10 per cent sales tax off drugs. There was great fanfare as that was going to mean lower drug prices. It did not mean lower prices; it meant higher prices. The drug companies kept the money. They did not reduce their prices a nickel.
I return to my main argument. The government has to decide and tell the people of Canada that it is no longer a universal program. Don't give me this nonsense about we are going to send everybody a cheque and then tax some or all of it back. That is the perverted part of it. It then becomes not universal.
I do not understand. I guess all political parties are guilty of this: The longer they are in, the harder they work at losing. Far be it from me to advise Conservatives how to stay in power. This is another one of those idiotic, unreasoning, nonsensical attempts by the government to pay the country's bills. I am not objecting to that. There is no one in the NDP caucus objecting to us making extraordinary efforts to pay our bills, debts, and our current deficit. No problem. That is not the argument. The argument is: how do you go about collecting the
money and how do you go about paying off and reducing the debt and the deficit?
I want to remind my hon. friends that at the end of the Second World War the national debt or the annual deficit translated into 1989 dollars was almost double what it is now, and we paid it off. We had relatively full employment. We did not have nearly so many tax loopholes, and we paid it off. We did nothing more than learn some lessons from our own experience in our own nation, that what we did before we could do again even better. There were other ways of doing it. By the way, not a nickel of the national debt at the end of the Second World War came from outside of Canada. We did the whole thing ourselves, and we paid off that deficit and that debt. By 1955 it was paid.
We do not have to claw back on the backs of old age pensioners and families with children, no matter what is their income. We must keep it universal and collect it some other way from those with higher incomes. Do not mess around. Do not try to destroy something that people of all political faiths since the 1920s have supported and agreed to. It is the only decent, civilized thing to do. It is for the government to say: "All right, we will withdraw this one. We will bring in some other measures to get the same amount of money". In that event we would likely support it.

Madam Speaker, I must say I am delighted to have the opportunity to speak tonight on this bill. I have heard many speeches in the House today on the subject of Bill C-28. There certainly seems to be a general theme, and the theme seems to concern all the speakers with about the same amount of amplitude.
We all know that Bill C-28 makes 59 different amendments to the Income Tax Act, implementing many of the budget provisions. Now it is not possible, of course, to speak on all these. There are some that concern me more than others.
I want to set a scenario which is perhaps a slightly different approach than some of the previous speakers have taken this evening. I do this with cognizance of the fact that aspects of the clawback are of concern to seniors as are the deindexation factor and the misrepresentation, if I can call it that. However, it is important to set the the stage by mentioning some of the things that
November 20, 1989

are going on in my riding right now against which people judge these 59 changes.
I have a situation now in which the telephone virtually has not stopped ringing in my riding. I just took some calls a few moments ago when I was talking with my constituency office. Literally the phone is just ringing off the hook. People who are listening to the speeches in the House of Commons tonight and watching them on television are concerned about these changes in the Income Ikx Act. They are concerned about many of the things that we have talked about here. It is so important to understand what their basic concerns are at this point in time, and to understand that I have to tell the House about my riding.
If not the largest fishing riding in Canada, my riding is certainly one of the largest where 85 per cent of the employment comes from the fishing industry. A month before Christmas, and we are now concerned, literally, that people have bread on their table and a cup of tea to drink.
I am referring to the emergency response job development program recently announced by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. I cannot tell you the number of people who will not qualify under that program although they have been employed in the fishing industry all their working lives, 15 to 20 years. Because of the criteria that has been set up it is not possible for them to qualify to get unemployment insurance under the job development programs. Because of the stringencies in the requirements and the inability right now of the bureaucracy to review those people they cannot fall directly under the criteria.
It is all very well to talk about the income tax changes and about all the difficulties we are going to have with clawbacks, deindexation and family allowances, but it is against the backdrop of people who will not have any money in their pockets to buy Christmas presents for their children, to make a Christmas cake, or to feed themselves when Christmas day comes. That is not a very nice thought as we talk about those issues in the House today.
While I feel it is incumbent upon me as a member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception to talk about Bill C-28, my major concern today and for this week is to get some kind of redress against the stringent criteria that has been set up and the lack of review process that has not been going on, although the Minister of Employment
Government Orders
and Immigration in fact stated in her press release that it would go on.
Let me talk just a little bit about the clawback. The clawback does a number of things, but what it does more than anything else is remove the rug from under the faith that Canadians have in what their politicians say and what their politicians from all sides of the House promise them during election time.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition and several members here in the House tonight reminded us of a lady by the name of Solange Denis who was so concerned about deindexation and a promise that was made which was not being kept that she became, if not a heroine, somebody who represented the concerns of the seniors in Canada.
In my riding there are around 10,000 senior citizens, all of whom either watched that or heard about it. They believe that what she did was so responsible and so representative of their feelings that even as I was campaigning last fall and I mentioned her name people remembered who she was. They remembered that television clip of that lady standing in front of the House of Commons and making a statement to her Prime Minister that she was being let down.
Common sense prevailed and deindexation was, we thought, forgotten about. The Prime Minister of the day said that universality was something that they would not have to worry about. They were going to make sure that these programs were universal, but our finance minister announced the clawback mechanism in his April 1989 budget which effectively ends universality.
The family allowance program and the old age security is paid to everyone now. Everyone receives the benefit regardless of income. Clawback, however, will recover the full amount of the benefit from those earning a certain income through a higher income tax rate. I refer now to clause 48 of Bill C-28 which implements the clawback on family allowance and old age security pensions. The amount of the repayment is equal to 15 per cent of the taxpayers' net income over $50,000.
The Minister of Finance introduced the measure as a deficit reduction device, but the amount to be recovered by the clawback is relatively insignificant when compared to the massive national debt. In fact somebody worked out that the same amount of money that is going to be realized by the clawback could be generated by raising the rate of the top income tax bracket by only 1 per cent,

November 20,1989
Government Orders
thereby transferring what benefit this would have to the deficit to high-income earners.
Many view the mechanism as discriminatory since it taxes pensioners and families at a higher rate than others earning the same income. Mr. Speaker, a buck is a buck is a buck. Why should people with families and people drawing old age security pensions be penalized more so than somebody else in a different age bracket or somebody without a family?
They do not understand why and, quite frankly, I cannot explain it to them, particularly since there was a promise made of universality and that these programs would be a sacred trust. I did not want to use that word because I think it is overused, but I have to use it to emphasize the promise that was made to Canadians.
Of greater significance and concern is that over the years more and more pensioners and families will start repaying these benefits. People have put together their savings, they have worked out their RRSPs, and they have worked out their investment programs. While $50,000 may seem like a lot of income for a senior citizen, many of the people in my riding-and I can assure you that there are those who do have that amount from a combination of their pension and their investments-have proceeded on the basis that they would be receiving this income and have projected their whole life after retirement on this assumption. Now they are told that they are going to have to rework the whole system. They are going to have to redo the whole thing. Their whole plan of financing will have to be reworked. The whole business will have to be redone. In other words, they are not getting the income that they had expected or that they had hoped to get.
Partial indexation is responsible. The threshold is now $50,000, but it has been calculated that by the year 2000 it will have fallen to the equivalent of $35,000 in today's dollars. That is 10 years from now. By the time the baby boom generation enters retirement, most of them will have to repay their old age security benefits through the clawback.
Is that fair? I do not think it is fair. I know that many of my colleagues do not think that is fair. I know that other members who are not my political colleagues but whom I have come to know veiy closely in the last year or so do not believe it is fair. I would suggest that there are many people on the other side of the House who do not believe it is fair either, although I have not heard too many of those this evening. I believe they will have to explain to their senior citizen population and to those who are drawing the family allowance as to why they think it is fair. It is going to be a difficult thing to explain.
In the meantime, once we have accepted the principle of clawback as part of our system, governments of the day are free to set the threshold at any they wish. The principle has how been established. It is $50,000 this year, and we know what will happen by the year 2000 if nothing is changed. But next year, if the government decides that more money is needed to address the budget or for another reason, the threshold could be changed to $45,000, to $40,000, or to $30,000. Who knows? I have not even heard any promises that this threshold will not be breached.
There are also widespread fears that the clawback is the thin edge of the wedge, a wedge that will destroy our much envied universal social programs. This country has been very proud of the way it has treated its senior citizens, certainly over my lifetime.
I know that seniors have been very proud of that. They have spoken to me about it. I know it has been a source of security and pride to senior citizens who have travelled outside the country and compared their lot with seniors in other countries. They have been able to say: "My government is proud of me and I am proud of it because it has been able to provide this universal service to me and it has been able to provide it in an unfettered manner with no strings attached". That is all gone.
History will remember the clawback as the end of universality, and not for what it has done for the deficit. My colleagues and I have been concerned that the government has not held any real public hearings on this issue. We have heard about the goods and services tax. We have heard about legislative committees on Bill C-21 and other legislative committees, but there has not been very much discussion about this issue. There has been a

decision. It has been capped at $50,000 with a 3 per cent limit on deindexing or indexing or whatever you want to call it. It does not look very good for the future as far as seniors are concerned.
Again, I do not know how to say this any more eloquently or with any more colour than I believe that senior citizens have and should have a very special place in all our hearts. Let us face it, if it were not for them a lot of us would not be here today. I would suggest most of us would not be here today. However there is a general feeling that when you reach a certain magic age something magic happens.
That may be the case, but in my riding there are many senior citizens who continue to make a contribution and to do things that they did before they reached the magic age. They do not look at themselves as much different from you and I or anybody in this House. They think they are average people who need to have average chances, who need to have the average opportunity to take advantage of all the programs that are in existence. They do not understand why they have to be made special by having money taken away from them more so than any other segment of society. I cannot go home and explain that to them, and I do not think anybody in this House can.
There is another area that concerns me and that is the income surtax on individual incomes. It has been raised from 3 per cent to 5 per cent and to 8 per cent for high income earners. Clause 47 of this bill raises the surtax on personal incomes from 3 per cent to 5 per cent. It also raises the surtax to 8 per cent for Canadians whose tax payable is more than $15,000. The minister made the proposal that personal income surtaxes would be a permanent feature of the income tax system. Essentially, what the minister said he was going to do is not what is being done. Therefore we have universality which is not being done and then we have the surtax increments which are not being done. What else is not being done?
Since 1984 this government has increased taxes 31 times. There are 59 clauses in this particular bill now. Canadians have not received the lower income taxes promised. In 1984 and 1985 the federal government collected $29 billion in income taxes from Canadians. This year the government expects to collect over $50

The clawback of family allowance will take $1,686 billion out of the family budget in the next five years. That is around $500 million a year by 1991. Perhaps I can take you back to the scenario I set earlier this evening, Mr. Speaker, to those people who could not spend all their time in the fishery because of a bad year in 1988. Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight on the eve of the anniversary of last year's election on November 21. Today is November 20, and I rise to speak on a bill which is very indicative of the kind of bill that this government has brought in since that election victory. This bill is an omnibus bill dealing with a lot of matters related to the changes in acts affected by the spring budget.
It speaks to the kind of deception this government perpetrated on the Canadian public in last year's election campaign. That is why I bring it to your attention on this date, the eve of the anniversary of the election.
This bill deals with the amending of the Income 'fax Act, including the clawback of family allowances and old age security pensions. It deals with the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act. It deals with the Old Age Security Act. It deals with the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act. It deals with the amendments to many of those acts.
Basically it allows for the opportunity to highlight the record of this government in all of these areas. We can speak to the contrast of what government members said during the election campaign and what they have actually done since they were elected. This is the government of deception.
The clawback of family allowances and old age security pensions on incomes of over $50,000 which the government introduced in its May budget and presented in this bill is a major step toward the Americanization of our social programs and the end of universality. This is exactly what Conservatives said they were not going to do. They said that we should not be worried about the trade deal, that it was only a trade deal and we could tear it up if we did not think it was a good deal.
We in the opposition spoke out strongly against the trade deal seeing it in its insidious nature as affecting our social programs. Here it is a year later. The government has invoked closure on this bill to do that, to really erode the universality of our social programs.
The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have tried to deny this, but the hon. member for Mississauga South was more honest. In a letter written to an
Edmonton man he said: "We have decided to eliminate universality. While the clawback may be unfair and sneaky, it is there." That is the nature of this government, unfair and sneaky in plain words but very descriptive.
For the first portion of my speech tonight I am going to focus on the effects of post-secondary education. I come from the province of British Columbia where we now have our premier in the light of recent events in eastern Europe trotting off to Europe and saying that he wants to get East German skilled labour and bring them back to British Columbia.
Are there not enough British Columbians already quite capable of taking the trades training that will be able to give them the kind of jobs that Mr. Vander Zalm is seeking for them? Federal transfer payments to post-secondary education are being eroded and the Social Credit government in British Columbia with the short-sighted vision of Mr. Vander Zalm thinks it has to bring in immigrant labour from overseas to fill the jobs we have in British Columbia.
Post-secondary education across Canada is being eroded by these cuts to this program under this Bill C-28. Now we spend something like $13,000 on average per student, while in the United States the average expenditure per student is $20,000. This is quite a difference. The Prime Minister promised to make education a high priority with reforms that will generate excellence in education from coast to coast. That was from the Progressive Conservative general meeting in August of this year. At the same time his government's latest budget reflected his real commitment to education as one of the priorities for its second mandate. These transfer payment cuts are going to have a devastating effect across Canada, but particularly in British Columbia where the Social Credit government has the shortsightedness not to put in the kind of funds that are necessary.
I now want to talk about some of the fundamental questions that should be asked when considering this type of legislation. Why should an individual be entitled to receive $100,000 in capital gains tax free but lose the $4,000 he or she will get in Old Age Security simply because it was paid as the universal social benefit? I am pointing out that if you get $100,000 through capital gains you are not taxed on it. But if you get it as part of a
November 20, 1989

pension you will have to pay $4,000. It is an erosion of the universality of our social programs.
The government members chided New Democrats for looking after the wealthy by voicing our concerns on this bill. What we are talking about is the fundamental injustice of this bill. Mr. Blenkam said it was unfair and sneaky. Those are the words that we will have to keep in mind in the final hours of this debate.
The family allowance and the old age security are already taxed in Canada. Why should a special tax be levied on children and the elderly? If the intention is to raise money from the rich why not do it through a more progressive tax system? I know that is the kind of thinking that is somewhat offensive to this government in its current bid to get the GST pushed through. Why not raise marginal rates at the top of the income tax bracket to 32 per cent instead of taxing back family allowances and Old Age Security? Either method would raise about $600 million in 1991. Why not restore the 1987 top rate to 34 per cent and raise $2 billion? The highest income group in Canada has its marginal tax rate cut from 43 per cent to 34 per cent in 1981 and to 29 per cent in 1987.
For middle-income earners the marginal tax rate has remained almost constant in spite of so-called tax reform. We on this side realize that the government must gain revenue especially in light of the trade deal when $13 billion in tariffs was lost through this government's signing of the trade deal. We realize that there have to be taxes. We are just questioning whether or not they should be coming from the same people, the low and middle-income earners, families and old-age pensioners. What will the unique identity of Canada mean in a few years when our social programs exist to serve only those in need. Won't our social programs be just like those in the US, leaner and meaner?
I had the privilege of travelling with the external affairs committee last week in New York and Washington. I saw on the streets of New York and in the city of Washington evidence of a leaner, meaner social program. There were beggars in the streets with tin cups. These are not just cartoon characters, this is reality.
Government Orders
Up here it is reality as well. This situation will only get worse under this government. How long will the population continue the maintenance of social progress from which they have been effectively excluded as beneficiaries? What we are concerned about here is the kind of erosion of public consent to participate in these programs. If it is only to be the low income earners who are the beneficiaries, why should the middle income earners contribute to them? We have a voluntary compliance system of taxation in our country. So far this government's policy, in this budget, through Bill C-28, and with its goods and services tax proposed legislation, is eroding that. What we are going to see are taxpayers very seriously trying avoidance schemes. This will have a real impact on the attitude of those who are recipients of social programs.
Social programs have been paid for. Old age pensioners have paid for this. They have been taxed on their income. Now they are having it clawed back under this bill. Will need be redefined downwards as it has been in Britain, or in the U.S., as it already has been in our unemployment insurance and welfare programs?
If the essence of universality is destroyed through the back door, what is to protect medicare from the same attack? We see the insidious nature of this government, the kind of deception in what it promised last November 20, and what it is doing this November 20. It is like night and day. I think this also speaks to a real lack of trust if this government is allowed to get away with the lies it has told Canadians on this and other issues. What effect will it have on the cynicism Canadians already feel toward politicians of all stripes?
I think that will have implications on our whole political system. I do not want to dramatize this overly, but it is a concern. It is the kind of cynicism that is everywhere throughout this country and it does not necessarily relate to whether it is a member of Parliament or the alderperson or the member of the legislature who is doing a good job. That, of course, has an impact, but the people do not trust politicians. One wonders why. But contrast what was said last November 20 and see where we are today. We are putting forth all the things that the government said it was not going to do.
There is no question that this clawback puts an end to universality. The National Council on Welfare which is a federal government advisory group is saying there is no

November 20, 1989
Government Orders
question but that the clawback puts an end to universality. This report was made to government entitled "The 1989 Budget and Social Policy" and states: "A social program that delivers benefits to everyone and then collects them all back from some recipients is not universal". I know that sometimes it is a difficult concept for some of the members opposite to understand when they say that it does not have an effect on universality. But when you give to some and take it away from some, that is an effect on universality.
The clawbacks are designed to save the federal government about $500 million a year. The savings would then be used to reduce the deficit rather than increase the benefits for low-income parents and seniors.
The National Council on Welfare has taken a page out of the New Democratic books and would prefer to see the government raise taxes for upper income people generally rather than having the heaviest burden on upper income parents and upper income seniors. Alternatives to clawbacks that are outlined in the report would save the government $2 billion a year, rather than $500 million.
I think we should also point out that this is a government that gives a lot of lip service in support of the family. While it gets a lot of Brownie points for those nice words, this bill erodes the whole concept of the family.
In the case of parents, the clawback discriminates against one-earner families because it is based on individual net income. A one-earner family with two children and a net income of $56,000 would lose all of its family allowance benefits. A two-earner couple where one spouse earns $45,000 and the other $35,000 would escape the clawback despite their combined income of $80,000.
Now, as I said, this government does give a lot of lip service to the support of families and about the way children should be raised, that women should stay home and look after their children rather than going out into the workforce. Well, here is a real slap in the face, because it is penalizing families which do that very thing. That kind of inconsistency is a bit galling to say the least.
I would like also to talk about the complexity of this bill regarding the child benefit system. After the clawback there will be four types of families receiving family allowance: Those keeping all of the family allowance because they are too poor to owe income tax; those families who keep part of their family allowance because they pay regular income tax on their benefits; those who keep part of their family allowance because they pay regular income tax and the clawback on their benefits and those who pay all of their family allowance back because of the clawback. This is a real distinction and we are talking about universality. It is a joke.
The clawback will erode the principle of horizontal equity. Removing family allowance from families that are better off will put them at greater disadvantage, vis-a-vis, childless couples and singles who have the same income but no child rearing expenses. Once again, this government gives a lot of lip service to the support of the family, but that is all it is, lip service. Its real motivations were veiy apparent in Bill C-28.
As members of an opposition party we have not only a right, but a duty and an obligation to oppose legislation that we believe is wrong-headed. We also have a duty and an obligation to propose alternatives.
As I said earlier, there is a recognition, even by New Democrats, that the deficit is a problem. We think it is an over stated problem, but if there are ways in which we can help advise these government members on how to address this problem, we are happy to try to contribute to that.
I believe the deficit has been over-sold to Canadians due to the Conservative ideology and the free trade agreement.

Lowering the deficit should be a goal of a much broader economic strategy not the only goal. That sort of linear thinking of the government members is apparent by this type of legislation. We have to think of a broader economic strategy. The government member opposite is eager to hear of our alternatives, so I am sure he will be attentive. I have not fallen to the cynicism of some of my constitu-

Canadians deserve a federal budget that responds to our real economic needs such as spreading the near full employment of southern Ontario to our regions. Ultimately, a focus on jobs and fairness will bring down the deficit. I think that should be the real focus of this government, a full employment program and a fair and simpler tax system. Then we would not have the erosion of the universality of our social programs as in this bill.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in this debate tonight, and I may add that tomorrow is the anniversary of the Tory Government's re-election. It was a sad day last year, when the Tory Government came to power for the second time. I am sure you remember that at the time, the Tory Government laughed at the Opposition parties with their various programs and said that Canada could not afford the kind of government being proposed by opposition members and the opposition parties. However, the Tories claimed they had all the funds that were necessary to continue to administer this government. That is what they said. They also said their commitments were not mere campaign promises but were backed with the necessary funds to implement them.
A year ago, it was the day before the election, November 20, 1988, and today it is November 20, 1989. One year later, suddenly the government no longer seems to have the funds it had last year. And to rely on the party's-I beg your pardon, the government's-coffers- I get the words "party" and "government" mixed up, because the Tories have a tendency to confuse the meaning of the two words. So in the light of those facts, Madam Speaker, I am sure you will excuse me for making this mistake, but it is typical of the government opposite, and I am sure that you, as an impartial person, will understand. I am sure you understand what I have to say in this respect.
In any case, one year later, the Tories across the way no longer have any money. No money at all. They have to cut here, they have to cut there, they have to raise taxes for Canadians. None of this was mentioned.

The Tories say they need the money so badly and they are so broke that they have to invoke closure and make members sit during part of the night to get those funds right away. Not bad, for a government that less than a year ago had all the funds it needed to administer this country!
Even if we agreed with the Tories a year ago, we can now conclude that what they offered Canadians was poor government, because all of a sudden they no longer have the funds they claimed to have.

But the sad reality is that the government across the way was not telling Canadians the truth a year ago, and it continues not to tell the truth to the people of Canada. Now, a year ago it was claiming, as I said previously, that it had all the money necessary to administer its own campaign commitments. You see, Madam Speaker, campaign commitments are slightly different from campaign promises. Campaign commitments were the ones made by Tories and campaign promises were the ones made by the opposition during the campaign. The Conservatives identified those differences at that time. They further added that all the funds necessary to administer the programs which they were proposing were completely inside the government's budgetary envelopes and that they were already provided for by the Estimates and so on.

he had better listen closely. He and his colleagues should continue to try to administer the Federal Business Development Bank, and listen attentively to what we are saying.
As I was saying before I was provoked, the family allowance is taxable. Thirty per cent of family allowance benefits are already paid back to the government through the progressive income tax system. The government is claiming that we need in addition to this a clawback provision, to snatch back the funds which the taxpayers of Canada have been receiving. It says not to worry, it only applies to rich people right now, only those earning $50,000 a year and so on. It says all those people are rich and can afford to give their money back to the Conservatives. Personally, if I were rich, which I am not, the last people I would want to give my money to are the people across the way. That is another issue and we can discuss it at another time.
The point is that this $50,000 threshold is only partially indexed-hardly at all, as a matter of fact-and will erode to such an extent over the next decade that many people who are considered not to be wealthy at all will then fall into that group of people who will see their pension clawed back by the Conservatives in the unlikely event that the Conservative party will still be in power at the time. I say extremely unlikely, because as we all know the Conservatives will be turfed out of office by then.
The other unfairness is that the proposal would put a special tax on families with children and on seniors, a tax that does not apply to anyone else. One has to wonder why the government wants to attack seniors and families. Is it not bad enough that it has tried to attack everyone with the GST proposal? It had 80 per cent of Canadians displeased with the GST. Some Conservative members looked at this and said to themselves that this was not good enough. They said: "What we should do is try to get unanimity". Do you know how they went about that? They decided to make the other 20 per cent angry, the 20 per cent of the people who are still supporting the GST. Do you know what they did? They put out a trial balloon about taxing existing homes. They sure have unanimity. Now everyone is angry at the Tories, even the few people who previously supported the GST proposal.
Returning to Bill C-28, in which the government has successfully found another way to get a lot of Canadians angry with it, it has invoked a procedure which is most unfair. Let me describe the scenario. For a senior citizen with $70,000 in income, the principle of fairness would suggest that it should not matter whether you get your income from a government pension, the stock market or elsewhere. A $70,000 income should be taxed the same way regardless of from where it comes. After all, a buck is a buck. Why should it be taxed differently if people get money from a pension, stocks, bonds, or anywhere else?
The minister sits in cabinet responsible for many government programs. Why would he, being the reasonable person he no doubt is, want to agree with such a program? I understand the minister from Brampton is agreeing with that, but not our friend from Montreal who is listening to this.
The government clawback provision would single out people who receive family allowances and old age pension cheques for a special tax. Why do the Conservatives across the way want to tax people who receive pensions any more than anyone else? Is it not bad enough that they are taxing everyone, that they would want a special tax grab directly aimed at people getting a pension? Why would they want to do that, other than finding another way to get unanimity, getting 100 per cent of Canadians mad at them again? They are bound to succeed one more time.
They have managed to do it with the GST. It took some creative thinking in those last two weeks to get the 20 per cent of Canadians who still liked the GST upset, but now they have succeeded in doing that. One hundred per cent of Canadians are mad. The Conservatives are going to do the same thing with this clawback provision. They had many Canadians mad at them for their income tax proposals. Now the few people that were not too upset are going to be upset with the implementation of this bill.
That is why we in the Official Opposition have stood for Canadians. We have contested these measures. We have indicated to the people of Canada that we do not like this bill and that we are not going to vote for it. I say to the members across, just in case the Tory members across think for instance that this is merely a partisan remark that I am making, as unlikely as that could be, to

read from One Voice Seniors Network Canada Incorporated, which is a national organization representing senior citizens across this country.
This is not the member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell or someone who may perhaps be thought of being partisan by those people across the way, but what One Voice said: "If we want to maintain true universality we shouldn't tax benefits through the back door. Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this debate on Bill C-28, legislation which flows from the Conservative budget tabled earlier this year.
This bill deals with a number of issues of concern to all Canadians. It amends the Income 'lax Act and includes
provisions, which I will be coming back to in a minute, respecting the clawback of family allowances and old age security pensions and a capital tax on large corporations. It cuts the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements and federal post-secondary education and health contributions. It deals with the Old Age Security Act. It touches the Public Utilities Income Ihx Transfer Act and as well it amends a number of other acts flowing from the budget.
Because the time is limited, I want to focus on two or three aspects of this proposed legislation. I want to first deal briefly with the cut-backs in federal-provincial transfers for health and post-secondary education because this amounts to a very serious erosion in EPF funding. We saw just three years ago in 1986 another round of cuts in EPF funding. What this will mean for Canada's poorest provinces is devastating indeed. In fact, the four Atlantic provinces alone will lose $189 million over the next four years while the four western provinces, including my province of British Columbia, will lose some $633 million.

We have to do it and our only hope is that my hon. friends from the other side will recognize some of the very difficult times that this country is going through in the financial area and get behind us and help us determine the best way to go about putting this government in a position of financial security so that these social programs can remain in Canada and be the pride of Canadians and so all of us can walk out of here with our heads held high.

Madam Speaker, in rising to speak in this debate it is interesting that we are continuing with an approach we have seen now for the last year or so in this House in the way the Government approaches problems in this country. We are discussing a bill that is described as an act to amend the Income Thx Act, the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements, and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, the Old Age Security Act, the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act and a related act.
In listening to my colleague opposite opening his address to the House I heard him say that we are not debating universality. My point is that government members remain consistent, say one thing and do the other, because in fact we are debating universality. The unfortunate thing is that we are debating it under the guise of income tax and other tax reform. It seems to me that the people of Canada understood the problem of the deficit and certainly now more than ever before in our history
November 20, 1989

understand the importance of the debt which this government has been able to double in five years from $170 billion to $350 billion. Those are things that Canadians understand, but I would think what they would appreciate from this government is for people to do what they say they are going to do. If we are talking about reforms to the Income Tax Act that are going to result in clawbacks, what we should be saying is that we are talking about changing the social fabric of this country, the social support systems, and be very candid about that.
I was amazed to hear my colleague opposite suggest that the Conservative government has gone through hard times in the last five years and has had to make difficult decisions. Canadians have heard from this government that the last five years have seen unparalleled growth in this country, have seen the economy improve on the basis of good management. So, how can the government say that everything is moving ahead in a very progressive way under Conservative management, and then say at the same time that we are in a position where we have to look very harshly at social programs because we cannot afford to pay for them.
That is the key, and I think that is a very good point. If you want to change social programs you can always trap people by putting them into an embarrassing position. In my view, if there is a group of people in this country who should never be embarrassed it is our senior citizens. The senior citizens that I speak to in this country are embarrassed because, by dint of hard work and through very careful management of their funds, some of them have accumulated some money, some of them have been able to develop a capacity to generate $50,000, $60,000 or $75,000 a year revenue. Some of us in this House may do that over the years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: And you are saying that we should still give them old age security?

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the comments of people who are suggesting that there is something apparently wrong with having people making $75,000 or $100,000 a year and not paying their fair share of taxes. If that is the case what we should do is address the legislation that is particularly relevant. Let
Government Orders
us talk to the senior citizens of this country and ask if they are prepared to make all of these contributions and not be concerned about this chipping away of their security, because what is a threshold today that looks very high and perhaps only affects people with relatively high income could, in a very short of time, change significantly. If we want to do this to them I think we should be telling them directly. There is no one better organized in this country than senior citizens through their senior citizens clubs, through the New Horizons Program that this government supports which previous governments instituted.
Let us go and ask them. Let us not embarrass them by forcing people making over $50,000 a year to have to fight this battle. They have fought their battles in this country and they have paid their taxes over the years in this country, they do not deserve to be put in the very awkward position of trying to fight this legislation on the basis that somehow they appear to be trying to hang on to what people would describe as too much money.
I am not going to debate whether or not the government should change its approach to how it takes care of people of 60, 70, 80 and 90 years of age. But if you want to do something, all Canadians expect is to be told what you want to achieve. Do you want senior citizens to pay down the debt? Do you want senior citizens to reduce the deficit? Ask them. Tell them. Do not say it is because you have too much and we want to take some away from you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: No, that is not what we are saying.
What are you saying, then?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: What is being said is that what has been given to you is only deserved if you have an income that is less than what it takes to live on.

The point that I am trying to make is that I believe that senior citizens should have the same rights as anyone else in this country. I do not want to in any way appear condescending to senior citizens, but I think that many of them for all kinds of reasons that every member of this House should understand, do not feel that they can fight these big battles any more. They

November 20, 1989

have spent their time in the trenches. If I am wrong, then senior citizens will tell me and will tell you, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: And they do.

I have been to Alberta and Manitoba and I have not had senior citizens saying: "My goodness I am glad that you have begun the process of eroding our security". I have not even heard people 50 and 55 years of age saying that.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: They have said: "We do not need it so tax it back".
I am sure that what-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I know what senior citizens in my riding are saying. I have talked to them.

Listening to members opposite I am sure that what they are saying is accurate to one extent. Senior citizens are generous. They do understand their commitment to Canada. Some of them would say that they would pay down, that they would pay their share if they had a few extra dollars. However, I opened my comments by saying that you say one thing and you do another. Is there someone, Mr. Speaker, to your right saying that the debt will be reduced next year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: The deficit will be, yes.
Mr. Speaker, is there someone to your right saying that the deficit will be reduced next year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Yes.
By how much?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: You will find out. Wait and see.

Mr. Speaker, one thing is for sure. We have been told by members to your right that the goods and services tax will be a deficit reduction tool, but in the very same document it states that it is revenue neutral.
The 23.9 is revenue neutral.
Mr. Speaker, the 23.9 is revenue neutral. The difficulty for Canadians-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: You are talking about old age security and whether people who earn over $50,000-
I wonder if the member for Gloucester might wish to make a speech rather have a question and answer period.

Mr. Speaker, I do not like to be rude to members opposite. It appears as though they have a number of things to say about this particular piece of legislation.
The difficulty that I have in listening to these comments-and I am listening to an hon. colleague from Alberta-is that they say that they are listening to people. Again, many of us are listening to what people are saying in Alberta. We do not even have to go out to Alberta to hear them because they are allowed to speak out in the presence of two members from your right, Mr. Speaker, in debate in the west on the goods and services tax, for example. Who are you listening to?
We are told, by members here apparently, that the population of Alberta must support the goods and services tax because members to your right support it, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
What does that have to do with old age
security?

It has to do with telling the truth. Who are you listening to? If you do not listen to people who do not like the goods and services tax, why would you be listening to senior citizens who do not like this approach to a clawback of what they have legitimately earned? Who are you going to listen to?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: We listen to everybody.

The point is that they say they listen when in fact they do not. They say it will reduce the debt when in fact it will not. They say it will reduce the deficit when in fact it will not. They say the debt that this country is faced with was created by mismanagement of previous governments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: It sure was.
When this government came to power the people of Canada owed $170 billion.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: It was $200 billion.
Today the people of Canada owe $350 billion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Interest on the debt.
November 20, 1989

What we do not accept is that people who will not understand simple arithmetic are talking to people and saying: "We are listening to them". You have not listened to people who say you have to reduce the deficit. The deficit is still over $30 billion a year. You talk about it but you do not do anything about it.
What I do agree with is if you are going to do something, then tell the people exactly what you intend to do. If you are going to tell senior citizens in this country that they have too much money and you want to tax them back, then tell them that, but do not tell them that you are going to reduce the deficit with their money because you have not been able to do that in the last five years.
Nonsense.
I listened to my hon. friend tell us that the income was now $16 billion more than what it was.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: You were not listening.
In 1984 they were borrowing $16 billion to pay for programs.
That is you.

That is right, our predecessors.
In 1989 there has been a $25 billion turnaround. That is what was said. The debt in 1984, when this $16 billion was being borrowed, was $170 billion.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: It was $200 billion.

What we will do is give members opposite the benefit of the doubt and we will say $200 billion.
Now, in 1989, after five years of good management, the debt is $350 billion. This is the kind of turnaround this government likes. The Conservatives are managing things so well that they have nearly doubled the national debt even according to their own admission.
To continue on the same line, what has been stated is that we could not afford some of these programs. This was stated by my friend just moments ago in his speech to this House. I quote: "Some of the programs we could not afford".

What we should do when we discuss this bill, Mr. Speaker, is have hon. members to your right get up and tell us which programs they cannot afford. That is what we need to know. It is not a question of whether senior citizens have so much money that you want to claw it back from them. If there are programs we cannot afford, there is one thing the people of Canada would like to be able to have and that is a straight answer on what it is that this government cannot afford.
It was very nice to listen to people opposite and perhaps we will get some answers to some of the things we are discussing tonight.
The element of attitude involved in all this debate on the kinds of directions that Canada is taking is illustrated when we, for example, listen to people in this House say that senior citizens are telling members of the government that they want this kind of a tax measure passed.
Are they speaking for associations of senior citizens? Are they talking about senior citizens' clubs across this country in the provinces of Quebec, British Columbia and Atlantic Canada? Are they getting petitions from senior citizens saying: "Please start this process of eroding the security that we always felt was ours and that was a guarantee in Canadian society"? Who are they listening to?
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that members to your right who have been here for more than six years have security.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I have security.

I listen to my friend say: "I have security". Is the hon. member comparing herself to a senior citizen now? There are different kinds of security. For many years in this country Canadians believed that they had security.
The Prime Minister of this country guaranteed Canadians security by saying that universality was a sacred trust.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: At $50,000 you are still secure.
Is it a sacred trust at $50,000, $35,000 or $25,000? Or, did we miss part of that phrase: "It is a sacred trust but there is a threshold to my sacred trust".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
They are still getting it.

November 20, 1989
Government Orders

They are still getting it, but he who giveth also taketh back.
We are going to have all kinds of opportunities to talk about the undertakings we have made to Canadians as legislators. We are going to have to decide when people are going to talk to Canadians-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: At $50,000 a year you still get $325 or so a month old age security, so let's get the facts straight.

There is no question that the intervention being made by my colleague is part of the ploy whereby you can say to Canadians: "Come on, can you be serious about questioning people paying back their fair share when they receive over $50,000 or $60,000 or $70,000 a year?" That is the crack in the sacred trust. It is the beginning. Nobody thought that they would simply get rid of old age pensions, or get rid of family allowance, or cut back on post-secondary education. It is: How do you start the process? How do you begin to convince Canadians that you are not going to be able to live in this country under a set of social standards-
What we are doing is convincing them that they will be able to live in this country.

I am looking forward to hearing those convincing arguments. I know the one argument that works in this House: a majority government defeats the opposition. That argument comes up whenever there is a vote.
Right.

There is no question that my colleagues across the way are right. When you have a vote, you lose. There is no question about that when there is an elected democratic majority.
Perhaps there is another consideration, though. It is how the majority got to be the majority. What was said to get them there? Sacred trust gets you there. Breach of sacred trust can move you out of there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Just like wage and price controls.
You know something, today-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Do you remember that one?

Yes, I do indeed.
Today, this very day, I heard the words again: "wage and price controls". Several months ago in this House I heard the words: "wage and price moderation".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: So it's moderation now.

The hon. House leader also heard the words: "wage and price moderation". This very day I had someone ask me "what do you think the chances are of the government introducing wage and price controls", all I could say was that I asked the question a couple of months ago-

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: You should know. What did you do with them?
Mr. Trudeau introduced wage and price controls-
After saying that he wouldn't.

That is right. There is no question that governments have often said one thing and done another.
I want to tell you one thing, Madam Speaker. It is a very easy thing to say that we are going to point a finger at what was done 10 or 15 years ago and to say that because they did it you would do it also. My question tonight to my friends opposite is very simple. Are you going to do it? We know what the Liberals did 10 or 15 years ago. What are you cooking up? Wage and price moderation sounds a lot better.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: We are cooking up a country that will be able to operate soundly for decades to come. That is what we are doing.

Madam Speaker, apparently we have the answer.
I want to say in closing that no matter what government says it or what political party says it, you keep saying one thing and doing another. One thing is going to happen to you is what has happened to governments before you that did the same thing.

Madam Speaker, I have a little problem here tonight. The member for Winnipeg South has departed the chamber. For the last hour or so she has been carrying on a heckling session with members on this side when they were speaking. One would think that if she had anything useful to say she would go on the record publicly and all the folks watching TV could hear what she is saying because it is forward into the past when she speaks. That is one comment I have. The other one is: I do not know for the life of me what it is that infects politicians once they become the government.

And you never will!

November 20, 1989

I suppose that the late I. F. Stone was probably right when he said that government is run by liars and nothing they say should be believed. He was right then, and as I watch it today it is true. I. F. Stone was right.
We saw examples of that. Liberals were running an election in 1974. They ran against Stanfield with wage and price controls. Once they became the government we got wage and price controls.
The Conservatives made a whole list of promises and commitments and as soon as they formed a government they broke every one of them. I do not know what it is. Maybe there are some microbes over there in the desks that crawl up their legs, up their ankles, up their knees, up the main part of their body right into their ears. It invades the brain.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: What is your excuse?

I have never been in the government so I cannot claim to have any microbes.
I hear the member for Brampton. It is fairly obvious that a cuckoo is resident in his head.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: I'd rather have a cuckoo than a woodpecker.

A woodpecker would have a heyday with a cuckoo.
On this question of the old age pensions, it is not surprising that they would have in clause 48 this clawback. They were never committed to pensions in the first place. Pensions were first introduced into the House of Commons in 1926.
I want to remind members of this House and the people who are watching that it was first of all $20 a month payable at age 70 and it was means tested. The Conservatives opposed it, Madam Speaker. They opposed a $20 a month old age pension payable at age 70, and it was means tested. What was the argument that the Tories used at the time? Can you guess the argument?

That it was not enough?
Government Orders

No, of course not. They said that paying 70 year olds $20 a month, not means tested, would make them lazy and would take away the initiative to work. Those are not my words. It is in Hansard. It is true. In fact, they should go back and look at the record. It got passed in the House and went to the Senate. The Conservatives in the other place defeated it and an election ensued in the course of things. Then the bill was brought back and eventually passed.
You mean a Conservative Senate defeated it?

That is right. And you know how they are all for work over there. They have a commitment to that ethic of work over in the Senate.
I only use that example to sort of remind us as we are discussing this whole question of universality and the clawback that these are people who really have no role to play. Conservatives were opposed to any social program. They are. The record is clear.
On the other hand, in this particular bill-and I want to raise this question very, very seriously-it seems to me that there is a fundamental change in the direction of this country. The record is clear that this party, the New Democratic Party, and its predecessors, the CCF, really believed that in fact the vision of this country was one of collective responsibility; that in fact the reason we are social democrats was because we asked ourselves the question: "Are we our brothers and sisters keeper?"
The answer came back, yes, so it developed that we supported every move and oftentimes initiated moves to establish social justice. With social justice came in its practical application old age pensions, family allowances, unemployment insurance, health care and a whole host of other social programs.
Now what am I hearing today? I am hearing from the other side that that is no longer the case, that it is the triumphant individual. That is the philosophy that I hear from across the way. No longer is the question of collective responsibility what motivates our actions in this House, but rather it is the triumphant individual; it is me. We see that in this worship of the market-place. We see it in this whole question of their worshipping at the

November 20, 1989
Government Orders
altar of the market-place. They have liberated greed. It is in fact: "You have no limitations. You can do anything you want. As long as I am all right, Mac, I do not give a damn about anybody else." That is what it is.
I am not only suggesting but I am declaring; I am saying very clearly.
She is back.

I see the member from Winnipeg South is back. I will say to her face what I said while she was away. I wish she would take the opportunity to get up and put her thoughts on the record so that all Canadians can not only hear her but can see her in the flesh to really realize that there is a body, an entity who is actually saying these things.
What I want to say is that this government is fundamentally changing the pattern of Canada, the face of Canada, the vision of Canada. That was never placed before the people of this country. As a matter of fact, a year ago, on October 17, 1988, the Prime Minister said: "As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished by the government which is committed to social justice and fairness for all Canadians."
I remember in the campaign the Prime Minister had his poor mother up on the platform. He had his mother, his sister, everybody. There was his mother, and he said: "Would I do this to my mother?" Well, he just did. I want to say: "Hey, Mama, he just did it to you in clause 48 in Bill C-28. He did it."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: She does not earn $50,000.

I do not know what the Prime Minister's mother earns. I have no idea, but he did it. In fact, not only did he do it in setting these ceilings of $50,000. That is only for starters, because we are down the road. As a matter of fact, the seniors citizens' network of this country puts out a paper called One Voice, and I want to quote what it said:
In the meantime, once we have accepted the principle of the clawback as part of our system, governments of the day are free to set the threshold as they wish-$30,000, $20,000, etc.
There are widespread fears that the clawback is the "thin edge of the wedge", a wedge which will destroy Canada's much envied universal social benefits program.
Those are the words of the senior citizens of this country, the united senior citizens of this country; not an
isolated group in any one province. This is a national organization.
The Vanier Institute said that this destroys families, that it does nothing for family life. I wish all those people on the Tory benches who claim to be for life would only stop to ask themselves: "How do I practise my pro-life positions on the government side?" How do they practise it? Is it by cutting back all the social benefits that help the family, that support the family, that strengthen the family? Is it by chipping away at benefits for children? Is that how we show we love life? Is that how we show we are for children?
Michael Wilson said it, and we should never forget it. I am saying that social justice is not going to be meted out by the community. Michael Wilson said it is going to be meted out by the bloodless verdict of the market. That is what Michael Wilson said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I know my hon. friend does not mean to do this in the heat of the argument, but he should not, as we all know, refer to an hon. member in this House by his name. He should either refer to him by his constituency or his portfolio if he is in cabinet. I think that hon. member knows that.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member for Nickel Belt is quite aware of that. The hon. member has the floor.

I was just going to say, Santa Clawback said that these decisions are not going to be meted out by the community, but they are going to be meted out by the bloodless verdict of the market, except it is the victims of these cutbacks that are going to shed a lot of blood. There is no bloodlessness about what they have in mind.
I wish that the Tories would just simply be honest to their Tory roots with respect to these social programs. I always said when I was in a campaign against a Liberal and a Tory that I have no respect for Liberals because they have no principles, but I have some respect for Conservatives because at least they have principles. I might not agree with them, but at least they have them. Since they have applauded me, now comes the question: Will they at least be honest? Can you be true to the principle of truthfulness and really say what you are about, which is to destroy universality? Isn't that what you are really after? The Prime Minister denies it, the member for Brampton denies it, the member for Athabasca denies it. Why don't they simply stand up and say:
November 20, 1989

"Yes, we don't believe in universality and we want to start this process of de-universalitizing the programs".
I say to the Conservatives, be honest! Be true to your principles. You believe in the triumphant individual. Why don't you simply say every person is responsible for his or her own pension program. Why don't you just say it? Why don't you say that there is no responsibility for a system that creates votes to redistribute that vote? Why don't you just say it?
Because, Madam Speaker, it is the truth. It is the truth and the one person who tells it like it is, is the one person I have any kind of respect for now on the Tory benches and that is-I can't say his name-Blenkie. Everybody knows Blenkie. Now I think he is euphemistically known as the member for Mississauga South.
He wrote to a gentleman who had written to him regarding the tax back for the old age pensions, and this is what he said:
"With respect to your clawback matter I understand your concern," Blenkam wrote in response to a letter of complaint filed by 61-year old William Daly.
"We have decided to eliminate universality and we do that in a sense by the clawback in both family allowance and the old age pension."
"As you know, it has been a Conservative philosophy for some time that distributions from the state ought to go essentially to those in need. While the clawback may be unfair and sneaky, it is there."
That is the one Conservative who tells the truth. God knows he tells it in a very colourful way.
Where is he now?

Well, we all know he is cooking up another theft from the taxpayers called the grief and suffering tax. Madam Speaker, notice what has now crept into the lexicon: "that it will essentially go to those in need." As democratic socialists the system we fought for was a system that allowed people to maintain respect, that allowed people in their retiring years to live with some dignity. It wasn't the system that says, well, you have to apply and there will be a needs test and if you are really poor, we are going to give you charity. This is the philosophy of the triumphant individual. We are in an era of triumphalism. Let us not kid ourselves, Madam Speaker. This is what we are in and these are the
Government Orders
acolytes of triumphalism. They are the acolytes and here the Prime Minister denies that this is anti-universality.
With Pinocchio it was the nose. With this Prime Minister it is the chin. Somebody said you can always tell when the Prime Minister is not exactly telling the truth-he moves his lips. I wouldn't be so cruel, but the fact of the matter is why would he persist in saying that this is not a taking away of the universality principle when it is admitted at least by one honest Conservative that it is? At least let the Conservatives be honest. We can deal with something when it is out in the open. But to have this sparring over what they really mean is counterproductive.
So I say to members on the other side, let's go back to what we decided when we built this country with respect to social programs. Do not sit there like a bunch of sheep. Come forward, defy your Prime Minister, defy the Neanderthals in the front benches.

Madam Speaker, after listening to the various speakers, I really have the impression we are hearing a dialogue of the deaf. At the same time, it reminds me of a phrase used by the French to define politics. They say that politics is war in peace time, and if we listen to the debate in the House, it is clear this is a war of words.
If we consider what has happened in government during the last ten years, I think Canadians have reason to be disturbed. I repeat, the last ten years, because I am not blaming either party which was responsible for governing this country.
Nevertheless, when we consider the figures, and especially those covering the past five years, we see that in less than 20 years, a deficit that was quite minimal managed to go up to over $340 billion, and there were also the many tax increases we have had since then. Especially in recent years, we have had many new taxes that have put a real burden on taxpayers, especially those with an annual income between $25,000 and $50,000.
Madam Speaker, about two weeks ago, I met a number of businessmen, mostly in the tourism industry, in Vancouver, Calgary and Toronto, and our discussions were remarkably similar. Everywhere, businessmen are saying that the tax burden has become a real problem, and they know there is a problem. Everybody says it is unfair and inequitable, but they cannot say exactly where

November 20,1989
Government Orders
the problem lies. But they do realize that the tax system is unfair and inequitable, and they are right.
The last time there was an attempt at tax reform in this country was 25 or 30 years ago. That was when the famous Carter Commission report was tabled here in the House but, unfortunately, it was never published. One of my Montreal colleagues mentioned the Carter Commission's famous turn of phrase: "A buck is a buck is a buck". Whether you get it from your pension fund or from investment, or by any other means, it should all be fairly taxed. If it isn't, obviously the money will have to come from another source.
We have seen the many taxes introduced during the past five years put the main tax burden on the middle class, while our financial elite has enjoyed unprecedented tax benefits. It doesn't take a university degree to realize there is something fundamentally wrong with our tax system.
We now have a government making a decision that is unprecedented in our history since we first had social programs. They tell us that when our annual income reaches $50,000, we no longer deserve to get any benefits from the State. And the fact that people made sacrifices to earn this money and invest it over the years doesn't count. It doesn't make sense! And that is why Canadians are sending petitions from all over the country. There is not a single member in this House who has not received petitions or letters from people who have been seriously affected by the way the Government has decided to tax them. The subject is on everybody lips. What does it take to convince the Government that we need sweeping tax reforms?
It doesn't take a university degree, as I said before. It takes some common sense to realize that things have reached the point that we are asking for a revolt.
The middle class is so busy trying to survive and raise a family that it cannot afford tax experts or tax lawyers to find all those tax loopholes. The only class that can afford these frills is the financial elite. If we look at the legislation passed by the House during the past 20 years, we have to say that the governments in power during that time were legislating for the benefit of the financial elite. And if anyone can prove the contrary, I will resign
my seat. It's true, and we all are aware of this. We don't have the political guts to put an end to this situation.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Watch your blood pressure.
