Madam Speaker, I have just been interrupted by a member who doesn't know what he is talking about. He would have us believe that everything is beautiful, when we are looking at unprecedented deficits and very real problems. Do you think I am the only one who shows an interest in this matter and who is mad as hell? All we have to do is travel around the country as I did to realize that people have reached the end of their tether and that the only reason they do not revolt is probably because Canadians have never had a tendency to do so.
However, people do feel the burden, deep inside, and they are concerned. They are concerned when they see their elected representatives, like the Hon. Member who just left the House, who sits in the House as a Minister, turn away as though the problem did not exist. But the problem does exist and we will have to face up to that problem in the House pretty soon. The time will come when Canadians- It is quite true that they are getting petitions from all over the country and from all kinds of organizations that have had enough!
Like most Members here in the House, I represent the middle class, the backbone of our society. I am certainly not exaggerating when I tell you that they have reached
November 20, 1989

the end of their tether and want some justice in our tax system. They know and we know there are problems. It isn't easy, but we have to accept certain decisions, and the political will must be there. Let them have the courage to say they will introduce tax reform, genuine tax reform. And in fact, we could usefully embrace some of the principles defined by a man who was a hero in our history at the time of the Carter Commission.
It was recognized as a revolutionary document in several fields, one which demonstrated some basic principles, that regardless of income, whether from investments, capital gains, pensions, whatever, everything should be taxed. Even succession duties were removed. But many experts and economists say that such a tax is quite appropriate in a democratic country-it is another way of redistributing wealth. That is one of the principles. This document could be used as the basis for a real reform. But unfortunately neither your government nor the previous one implemented the main recommendations of the Carter Commission report, and that is what we must look at. I believe that my fellow citizens, like those whom I have met, who send letters on all sides of every issue, are telling us that we do indeed need a reform. They are quite interested in seeing a government live within its means.
But when they see the deficits and the taxes piling up, they realize there is a fundamental problem. They do not have to be great economists. How many of my colleagues here saw their parents during the depression years forced to make more sacrifices to avoid debt? They adjusted. And we have a long history which proves this ability to adjust. Now, can we believe for a moment that a national or other government can survive on the brink of bankruptcy, especially when the time comes to take such drastic action as cutting vital public programs? That would almost be admitting failure; it would almost mean bankruptcy. But what we must remember is that in this Chamber, we represent all classes of society and to a large extent the middle class which makes up most of the population. These people are saying that they can no longer bear the tax burden. So, our role is very simple. As all Members of the House know, and I am not the only one to say so, time will come when your own constituents will litterally knock at your door and tell you that changes are necessary, that a reform is imperative.

Otherwise, we will all suffer, and that is the fate awaiting us.
To conclude, Madam Speaker, I am sure that if every one of my colleagues here in the House took the time to ask their constituents-they do not have to do so since they receive letters-if every one of them was getting to the heart of the problem, they would see that most of the people are concerned and are counting on us to find at least a partial solution.

Madam Speaker, I only want to say a few words tonight on Bill C-28, which is an act to amend the Income Thx Act, the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act at this second reading debate.
I listened to some of the comments made by the last several speakers who had the floor. Quite frankly, many of the arguments, as the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt pointed out, go back to the time when old age pensions were first introduced in Canada, namely, that people should be self-sufficient. One of the arguments that I heard tonight was why should someone making $50,000 a year receive an old age pension?
I remember in 1985 when this government was proposing to deindex old age pensions, one of the arguments given then was why should bank managers and bank presidents receive old age pensions. That question has been answered both in the House in previous debates and by Canadian society generally. The reason why people should receive those universal social benefits is that they paid for them. That is the only basic argument; They paid for them.
If the government believes that because that individual received that social benefit, his or her income is too high, then there is another way to address that, namely, to bring in a fairer taxation system, not to attack a social benefit that is universally supported in this country and, indeed, can only exist if it is received on a universal basis. Unless society broadly supports that kind of program, it will fail. I think everybody is in general agreement with that.
Senior citizens have paid for those pensions. It is not something that governments give to senior citizens through the goodness of their heart that can be taken

November 20,1989
Government Orders
away at will. Senior citizens paid for the benefits they received. They paid for them through the income tax system in recent years. It is the same with family allowances. Both programs are already taxed when people receive them. Old age pensions are taxed as a part of income. Family allowances are taxed as a part of income. Why does the government feel it is necessary once again to go after senior citizens?
I remember in the last campaign I received a phone call from a very active senior in my community. I know she will not object to my using her name, Gerry Schwalm. Gerry called me the day after the Prime Minister was seen on national television with his mother assuring seniors in Canada that the opposition parties, the Liberals and the New Democrats were lying to them when we said that the first thing that would be attacked under free trade would be social programs. The Prime Minister pointed to his dear old mother and said: "Would I touch her pension?". Gerry Schwalm said to me: "That guy just scared me half to death. Every time I hear that guy saying that he won't do something to social programs, he is going to do it".
In 1984, this Prime Minister said: "Universal social programs are a sacred trust". It took him five months before he tried to rip them apart. On October 18, 1988, in Summerside, Prince Edward Island, another community that is going to appreciate this, the Prime Minister said: "Let me say a special word to the senior citizens. In the future in Canada we will be doing more not less for all of you. As long as I am the Prime Minister of Canada, social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved not diminished by our government which is committed to social justice and fairness for our Canadians". Some social justice and some commitment!
Seniors in this country trusted this government when they elected it in 1984. By the time 1988 rolled around there were not too many senior citizens in this country who believed the government any more. I would think there would be even less today after seeing what this government is proposing to do to seniors once again in this piece of legislation.
Senior citizens are not stupid. They know that when the government is talking about clawing back pension benefits for those who earn in excess of $50,000 a year
today, next year is going to be a different figure, and the year after that is going to be a different figure.
This government has never believed in the pension system. Since I came here in 1980,1 could count on two hands the number of times that that government has tried to go after the pension systems in this country. In fact, just prior to the last election, the Minister of Finance tabled a White Paper on pension reform in the private sector prior to the election. There was such an outcry in this country from organized groups that the government withdrew the White Paper, but it is still sitting there. The government withdrew it because it knew it was going to hurt in the election campaign. However, the White Paper is still sitting there and I will put money on the fact that before we get to the next election we are going to see it again. The Tories are not happy, and they are not going to be satisfied with just going after the public sector, they are going to go after the private sector.
I would recommend to every member in this House, especially the ones who were not here between 1984 and 1988, to get a copy of that White Paper and read it because that is the next fight on pensions.
Now, I said that I was not going to speak too long and I do not intend to. However, I do want to read something and I am going to do it very slowly because I want the government to take heed of it. It is a letter written to The Globe and Mail in Toronto by a senior who was recalling some of the recent history on pension plans and, in particular, how the Old Age Security Act was funded. This letter states:
Between 1952 and 1971, all taxpayers paid surtaxes to provide for OAS.
Between 1952 and 1971, Canadians paid a surtax to provide the old age pension. It did not run out.
Beginning in 1972, the Trudeau government made the surtax invisible and raised the tax rate by some 3 percentage points, with the funds raised going to general accounts-and this remains unchanged. Therefore, all old age security recipients have contributed towards this pension plan; they continue to contribute even during retirement; and, lest it be overlooked, such pension payments are included as taxable income.
And that is what this writer calls "double taxation".
Senior citizens have paid and bought and are still paying for their old age pensions. It is not something that somebody is handing to them out of the goodness of their heart. They paid for them. It is much the same argument we are facing from some members on the other side, not all members, but from some members
November 20, 1989

who seem to truly believe that somehow or other seniors are getting charity when they receive OAS and that that charity can be given or taken away at will. They paid for it.
It is much the same argument as was used by that government during the last Parliament when it went after civil servants' pensions, civil servants who, numbers of years ago, agreed to have 1 per cent of their income go to pay for indexation of pensions and this government tried to take it away from them. They had paid for it.
It is much the same argument that we faced from this government when we had amendments to the Pension Benefits Standards Act around 1987 when we dealt with surpluses and private plans. Who do surpluses belong to? Do they belong to the employer or do they belong to the employee? My argument is that they belong to the employee. They are deferred wages. They were negotiated in collective agreements. Those pensions were given up as a part of the wage package in order to provide that individual with a decent pension on retirement. Those moneies belong to the individual. It is no less the case with old age pensioners. They paid for the pensions. They bought them. They belong to seniors.
This government has no right to come along with this kind of legislation and try to grab that money from them. Describing what is happening in this bill as a clawback is absolutely right. It is an apt description of what this government is trying to do, if it gets away with it. It is a clawback. It is like sticking a hand in a senior citizen's pocket and taking money right out of it. That is what this government is doing.
I think it is insidious. I feel it is offensive. It is something I will not support. I would hope that by the time we get into a vote on this that members of the government side who recognize that what is happening here is wrong and should not be allowed to happen will join with the opposition to defeat this.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise and have the opportunity to add my voice to the voice of the opposi-
Govemment Orders
tion against Bill C-28 and to add my voice on behalf of the residents in my riding of Okanagan-Shuswap.
This is a fairly substantial piece of legislation. There are about 59 amendments contained in this omnibus bill and certainly I will not be touching on all amendments. I would like to concentrate on a few of them. To begin with clause 47, which is the increased surtax, I think a lot of Canadians do not even realize that virtually every Canadian who pays taxes in this country also is paying a surtax.
People across this country, particularly those who live a long way from Ottawa, out on the west coast for example, feel that the role of the federal government is almost indistinguishable from the role of the provincial government. They are a little confused with what the responsibilities of each of them are. I tell you, Madam Speaker, that breaks down when it comes to tax matters, particularly income taxes. When it comes to tax matters, everyone knows that it is Ottawa's hand that is in their back pocket.
A surtax is defined as an additional or an excessive load or burden in addition to ordinary income tax. In 1986 a surtax was introduced by this federal government on federal income taxes and the rate at that time was established at 3 per cent. It does not apply only to upper-income Canadians. It is payable by virtually any Canadian who is paying federal income tax. They are also paying a surtax.
The government makes the argument for the fairness of imposing this tax by saying that it will ensure that the burden of deficit reduction falls most heavily on those who are best able to carry it. That statement was made in this House recently by the member for Wild Rose and is recorded in Hansard. Obviously since the surtax is payable by virtually anyone who has a taxable income and not just by the top few who can most afford to pay it, the burden does not fall upon only the shoulders of those who can most afford to pay it. The argument of using higher-income Canadians for deficit reduction is a fallacy. It is a sham. It is like this government is a sham in what it is trying to do with this legislation.
The finance minister said that when this surtax was introduced it would be a temporary measure. We have heard of temporary measures before. The income tax I believe was introduced after the First World War as a

November 20,1989
Government Orders
temporary measure and we still are dealing with it. Just like the surtax was introduced as a temporary measure in 1986, we are still facing it.
A goods and services tax was introduced in the April budget. The finance minister said that when such a tax would be introduced the surtax would be removed. Instead, the surtax is being increased to 4 per cent for 1989 and to 5 per cent for 1990. There is no removal of this surtax. We are getting hammered once again. More is being applied. The GST has been proposed. Where is the provision to get rid of this surtax? Where is the promise that the Minister of Finance made at that time? I think the government is following the axiom of why spoil a good election promise by actually doing something about it.
Moving on to clause 56, this clause implements changes to our federal transfer payments to the provinces for health costs and post-secondary education costs.
The budget that we saw introduced earlier this year outlined a decrease in these payments over the next four years. In that time period the four western provinces will lose $633 million. What is this going to do to health care and education in those provinces? To British Columbians it is going to mean that all too familiar theme that we experienced after the recession in the early 1980s, during the restraint era of the Bennett government, the years that we are still tiying to recover from. The news of decreased federal transfer payments is not good news for British Columbians, is not good news for the residents of Okanagan-Shuswap.
A good education for our children, which is insured by these federal transfer payments when it comes to post-secondaiy education, is not just an expense, it is an investment. It is an investment in the future of this country. It is certainly an investment in the future of our young people.
Being wealthy is not relative to intelligence. Our best and our brightest will not necessarily be among the ones who can afford the best schools. Adequate funding for post-secondary education today, as we all know, is crucial to the future of all Canadians. Reducing these
transfer payments jeopardizes that future, it jeopardizes the future of our young people.
In the past Canada has had an exemplary health system. Today I think we would all agree that that system is deteriorating because of inadequate funding and also a tendency of governments to blame the users. Yet health care in Canada is a right. We do not want the American system in which hospital admittance is determined by one's ability to pay, and certainly not by the degree of illness or injury.
Let us turn to clause 48, which is one that most members have been focusing on over the last little while, and that is on the family allowance and old age security clawback, what the government calls a benefit reduction tax.
In the debate on bill C-28, it has been pointed out a number of times in the House that from the 1950s to 1971 people paid about 4 per cent of their income into the Old Age Security pension. My colleague who spoke just prior to me this evening said they have paid for this benefit. They were investing in their future, in their twilight years when people put money into the Old Age Security program. It was a contributory program and people did not mind paying into it because they trusted the government, and they believed that when they reached retirement age that money would be there for them.
Today, this government proposes to tax back that pension. What was paid for by those contributors then and through the years is now being taken away from them. It is being snatched back. It is being literally ripped from their back pockets. That is why seniors right across this country have lost faith and trust in this government. They have seen once again that it never lives up to the commitments it makes.
The Okanagan-Shuswap in the interior of British Columbia is in large measure a retirement area because of the climate and the geography. We have a large percentage of people who are over the age of 65. The demographics in the riding indicate that more than 15 per cent of the population in my area are seniors. The changes that this government is about to make with these clawback provisions will seriously affect the financial future of seniors in those communities. A lot of these retired folk do not receive over $50,000 a year in income, so they are not going to be affected initially. At the same time they have expressed to me in no uncertain terms their fears of what this process has initiated.
November 20, 1989

They recognize that today when this government sets the clawback threshold at $50,000, tomorrow that threshold may be lowered. I submit that it will be lowered to $30,000, perhaps even lower. Although many of the seniors will not be impacted by these changes, what about tomorrow? They know from what they have seen that they cannot trust this government and they are worried about their financial security as this government tries to rip away the benefits that these people have paid for, trusting that they will be there when they finally retire.
The Old Age Security clawback is based on the formula of inflation minus 3 per cent. As we saw in 1985, seniors fully understand the consequences of deindexing pensions. They knew what the government was up to when it wanted to deindex the pensions from keeping up with the inflation rate. They caught members across the House in the act of trying to quietly claw back those provisions. They stopped them then and what the government has done in an insidious way is come back at the problem again through the back door. It is trying to claw back these pensions by capping them at a higher level. It is a mean spirited provision and it is no wonder that seniors across this country have lost trust and lost faith in this Prime Minister and this government.
The Minister of Finance says that only 4.3 per cent of senior Canadians currently receiving the Old Age Security benefits will be affected by the clawback. That is in
1990.	In 10 years it will be up to 8 per cent. In 20 years it will be up to 25 per cent if nothing else is done and we all know that we cannot trust that nothing else will be done.
A 30 year old in the workforce today earning an annual salaiy of $30,000 will see part of his or her Old Age Security benefits clawed back by the time they retire. We are part of an aging population in this country and that which is of concern to seniors today will be of concern to all of us tomorrow.
I want to move on to the section on family allowances and the clawback provision affecting this benefit. Whereas seniors would need to have a net income of about $79,000 before they would fully lose their old age security benefits, when you look at the threshold for the family allowances that threshold is much, much lower. We have to remind members on the other side of this House why mothers are paid a family allowance. It is in recognition of the very real costs associated with raising children. Our children are our future. The future of those children, I think, is the collective responsibility of all of us in

Canada. Anyone who has children knows the significant costs a family bears in raising those little ones from toddlers to adulthood.
Today the family allowance is only a token payment. It does not begin to cover the real costs. The payments fall far short of what it costs to bring up a child. To tax back this token payment amounts to robbery. It constitutes a total disregard for the families and the children and the future of those children in Canada.
In the initial year of the imposition of this clawback, the first year in which it comes into effect, 14 per cent of Canadian families who now receive family allowances will be affected. In 10 years that figure is expected to double simply because of the inflationary aspect of it. In previous speeches in this debate it has been said many times that the clawback funds from Old Age Security provisions and family allowances will be used.
We have heard the government members talk about it time and time again. The argument they give is that those benefits will be used to help those Canadians who really need it, a noble gesture by all means. When you think about it and analyse it, it is totally illogical.
It has been stated also that the imposition of the clawback is for the purposes of bringing down the debt. How are you going to use it to bring down the deficit while at the same time you are using it to funnel it to those people who really need it? It is a logical consistency. The government is guilty of doublespeak on this.
The money that is refunded by the clawback tax is not going to be used to increase the benefits to those seniors and to those families that really need it. On the other hand the government is saying it is going into deficit reduction. In fact, when you look at it, more money for more people will be collected with this tax over the next few years because these benefits are only partially indexed. More and more people will begin to qualify for that clawback provision.
Seniors in this country want to pay their fair share. They want to tiy to help in the difficult challenge we have of deficit reduction. Families in this country want to do the same thing, but the emphasis here is on the word "fair". How is it fair when one group is singled out and must pay extra taxes when somebody else who is receiving the same income does not pay those taxes at all? A senior with an income of over $50,000 is now going to be subject to a clawback of those very benefits that he paid for years down the road. Somebody under the age of 65 making exactly the same salary does not have to pay that

November 20, 1989
Government Orders
tax at all. Is that fair? I suggest to you it is not fair. It is that this is only the beginning. This is only the beginning not fair in the least.	of the end.
Not only is it not fair but I also submit that it smacks of age discrimination. A seniors group has pointed out that the amount that the government is trying to save by not paying these Old Age Security benefits, by clawing them back, could in fact be collected by raising the taxes of high income earners in our country-the well-to-do-by one percentage point. We could collect the same amount without having to touch the Old Age Security provisions.
Much has been said on the violation of the principle of universality with the erosion of these social programs. The Prime Minister and his broken promises and I repeat, his broken promises, have been quoted by almost every member who has attacked this legislation. The quotes are memorable because they are so incredible. Whether it is only 4.3 per cent of seniors as the Minister of Finance contends or whether it is only 14 per cent of families that are going to be subjected to this clawback, any one person treated differently simply means that the concept of universality which the Prime Minister called a sacred trust is gone.
The government argues that the programs are still universal, that everyone still receives a cheque, but a number of the recipients have to return those cheques. The numbers who will fall under this category as I stated before will steadily increase over the years.
There is no question that this is the beginning of the end of the enshrined concept of universality the Prime Minister holds apparently so dear to heart. These programs are no longer universal, but they are by the intent of this legislation now selective.
I want to turn to one final point and I think this is probably one of the most salient issues in my arguments tonight because I think that one of the most telling points that comes out of the debates and the comments that we have heard throughout this evening is that there is something very elementary lacking, and that is the lack of trust in this government as a result of what it has done over its two terms. It is an oft-repeated comment, whether it is on this bill or the goods and services tax,
People trusted what was said by the Conservatives and this government. When they promised not to touch the social programs they believed them. People trusted the Prime Minister when he said that social benefits especially to the elderly would be improved. It would not be diminished. Those are not my words, those are the words of the Prime Minister. The Canadian people trusted him when he said that and I submit that that trust has been abused. Its sole purpose was to win votes. That trust is gone. Canadians no longer trust this government. Universality is gone, trust is gone and I hope that soon enough this government will also be gone.

Although it is getting late, Madam Speaker, I should like to deal briefly with this Bill, because we have just had a week off. Most of us, I think, spent it in our respective ridings. Madam Speaker, I am sure you too have constituents who are quite worried about the fact that the government is planning to raise new taxes. Canadians are complaining that they cannot make ends meet. This is the very first day we spend in the House. What are we dealing with? Taxes again. Taxes, whether sale taxes, income taxes, sale taxes on goods and services, all kinds of taxes.
As recently as this afternoon, because I had been unable to return all my calls, I tried to reach some of my callers from Ottawa. For instance, there was a lady who wanted to know if she could collect her child tax credit before filing her income tax return because she could no longer make ends meet.
Madam Speaker, it is easy for the Government, whatever its political stripes, to say that it must raise new taxes. It needs only introduce a new legislation. Can the old pensioner who does not have enough money seek more from the government? Can the worker who cannot balance his budget obtain a raise from his employer? I think the time has come for us to put a stop to this madness and behave responsibly. It is not the way to solve the problem. Madam Speaker, I realize that for the past five years, the government has insisted on the need to raise taxes to cut the deficit. But the deficit has not increased. As of March 31, 1984, according to the official statistics for the last complete fiscal year before this government came to power, the deficit amounted to $32 billion. But if we look at the Minister of Finances'
November 20, 1989

forecast for next year, we are still at $32 billion. After five years of an extraordinary economic performance, including 32 tax increases, the deficit still amounts to $32 billion, while the national debt will have tripled by the time this Government completes its second term. Thx increases, therefore, are definitely not the solution, and by the time the new tax is implemented in January 1991-

The GST will be imposed, a 9 per cent tax across the board, on everything. The government may try to tell Canadians that yes, you will pay 9 per cent on everything but the federal manufacturers' sales tax of 13.5 per cent will be removed. First of all, how is this going to happen. There is no way the government, if it is looking for control, is going to remove that 13.5 per cent.
Speaking of the 13.5 per cent, in 1984 when this government took office, the tax was only 9 per cent. In five years it increased it to 4.5 per cent. What guarantee do Canadians have that the new GST of 9 per cent will remain 9 per cent. Maybe in a few years it will be 20 per cent. Imagine 20 per cent or 9 per cent plus the provincial sales tax.
The government tells Canadians to look at the over 40 countries around the world that have GST or value-added tax.
But it forgets to tell Canadians that is the only tax, one sales tax. We have 11 sales taxes in this country. When you add all that together, Canadians cannot take it any more. It is very easy.
You do not have to be an economist or a genius to understand that Canadians cannot afford to pay tax any more. And what do we do? We take a week off. The major concern of our electors is stop increasing taxes. The first day that we come back, we have a bill and we have to stay late into the night because the government is in a rush and has to pass the bill because it needs the
Government Orders
money. Where will this money come from? It will come from the taxpayers.
The members on the other side might laugh, but I can assure them that in my riding and in many of my colleague's ridings, it is not a laughing matter. It is a very serious matter. Canadians are fed up. I would not be surprised if by the end of 1990 we will not have a tax revolt in this country because Canadians are fed up.
I do not want to take too much time of this House. I think if the Conservative members want to vote, I am sure that when the time comes Canadians will judge them. I want to make sure it is in the record that Canadians are fed up with tax increases and new taxes. I think it is time if the government wants to look seriously at the deficit problem and the debt problem, it should look elsewhere because in the past five years we have seen over 30 tax increases. After five good years of economic performance the annual deficit is at the same level as it was five years ago and the national debt is going to be tripled by the end of this term of the government.

Madam Speaker, I rise to participate in the second reading debate on Bill C-28, an act which has the effect of implementing the April budget of the government and in particular the provisions which will claw back, as the expression has come to be used, old age pensions and family allowances and which will cut back a number of important federal funding programs including the Federal Provincial Fiscal Arrangements, Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act.
We have heard a lot of anger in the House tonight. I share that anger and I know many of my constituents in Victoria share the anger at the government's approach on this particular bill and, more generally, the approach it is now clear it has been taking over the last year on a range of public policies for this country. This bill fits in the over-all program and agenda which the Conservative party is now foisting upon the people of Canada. That agenda started in December with the free trade legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext: (Vancouver Centre): Hurray.

We hear "hurray" from the member for Vancouver Centre. I am pleased to see the member for Vancouver Centre here tonight. I am looking forward to

November 20,1989
Government Orders
her rising in her place and challenging this legislation which is punitive to seniors, punitive to the poor, punitive to families in Canada, punitive to those who are trying to get an education in this country. So far we have heard silence from the Conservative members from British Columbia. I look forward to her intervention in this debate.
The clawback provisions of this bill are the Conservative's rebound from the political failure they met in 1984-85 when they tried more directly to end universality in old age pensions and in family allowances. They retained a small portion, even then, of their attack on universality because they allowed a certain amount of deindexing through the work of inflation. Now they have come upon a formula which has permitted them to destroy the principle of universality with relatively small outcry from the country as a whole. I believe the lack of response in the public is in part due to a defeatism brought on by the sense of loss that comes with the free trade agreement, a loss of the direction of this country, but also the sense that the Conservatives, with their majority, are driving through a reactionary and regressive agenda which is going to change the nature of this country over the next few years.
It took years, a fight led by parliamentarians such as J.S. Woodsworth and Stanley Knowles, to finally push the Government of Canada into introducing old age pensions in this country. Back in 1926, Mr. Woodsworth and his colleagues used the minority government situation to force a Liberal government to introduce old age pensions, but the old age pensions were then introduced with a means test. It then took over 20 years to finally persuade the Government of Canada to change that, and then it was not an act of generosity on the part of the Government and Parliament of Canada but because of the political threat from the CCF, as it then was, which had been pounding away at the issue on behalf of seniors that the means test was unfair and ungenerous.
Finally, the principle was established that as a right, Canadians were entitled to an old age pension. Rich, poor or middle income, irrespective of income, Canadians as Canadians were entitled to family allowances. These universal programs meant that we had a distinctive social network. They formed the base of our distinctive social network in this country which distinguished us from the country to the south.
Conservatives never did like universality. In fact, the member for Mississauga South who is the chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance and has this fall been regaling Canadians with a series of quotes, said in a letter to a Mr. Daley from Edmonton: "With respect to your clawback matter, I understand your concern. We have decided to eliminate universality". He went on: "As you know, it has been a Conservative philosophy for some time that distributions from the state ought to go essentially to those in need. While the clawback may be unfair and sneaky, it is there".
The Conservatives tried in an awkward and messy way in 1984 and 1985 to put their agenda into effect. Now they are doing it again with three full years before the election, greeting an electorate that is tired and worn down by the hypocrisy and reactionism of this government.
We are not going to allow this bill to pass without speaking out. The people of Victoria, and particularly the seniors of Victoria, have had it up to here with the broken promises of the government. This was the government, during the election last year in its attempt to defend free trade, which was forced to say, "This will not erode our social programs. Universality is a sacred trust". It did not take the government four months before it had broken that commitment to the seniors of this country and to the people of this country.
The Conservatives are, by this provision, changing the income tax law so that at a certain point, 100 per cent of income earned from old age pensions or family allowances will be taxed back. If you earn your money through dividends, salaries, capital gains or gifts, those are taxed, if at all, at a different rate. At a certain level, old age pensions are taxed 100 per cent.
This breaks faith with election commitments. The cynicism of the Canadian people continues to grow at the speed with which this government breaks its election commitments, but it breaks a long-standing commitment from this Parliament to the people of Canada who have tried to plan their futures as seniors on certain commitments coming from the Parliament of Canada. This government, instead of what we would say in the labour context of grandfathering the clause are in effect making a retroactive change. They are changing today the basic pensions which frugal, prudent Canadians over the years
November 20, 1989

have used as a base for planning their retirement income. I say that this change must not occur.
Let me deal with a couple of other aspects of this bill. The government has said that in this new free trade era, education is one of its major priorities. Yet this bill will have the effect of cutting back even further on federal support for basic education and for post-secondaiy education. This bill will permit the government to cut back on health care and on social assistance across Canada. It does so in the name of deficit cutting.
The seniors of Victoria, the people of Victoria, the people across this country, know that we cannot permit the deficit to continue, a deficit which has grown to mammoth proportions under this government. What we say should be the priorities in deficit cutting are not to be placed on the backs of the seniors or families or students or those involved in health care, the poor in this country, but instead we must attack the deficit in this way.
We must cut government waste. We must take a hard look at the $1 billion we are spending on maintaining troops in an outdated commitment in Europe. We must look at reducing interest rates. We must look at an eco-tax, at a wealth tax. We have to change the corporate tax rates in this country and we have to change the tax rates at the upper level.
This government has cut the tax rates at the upper levels. A simple increase to 34 per cent would add nearly $2 billion to the coffers of the government. That is what should be done instead of the kind of changes which are contemplated in this bill.
With the GST, with these clawback provisions, this government continues its agenda of eroding social programs, of creating two nations, a rich and a poor, of bringing us further into the same programs as our colleagues to the south of us have. We are now beginning to look more and more like the United States because of the agenda which this government is foisting on the Canadian people. I ask this House of Commons to defeat this bill when it comes to a vote later this evening.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on Bill C-28, an act to amend the Income Tax Act. Specifically, I would like to speak to the clawback clauses in the bill.
If I may, Madam Speaker, I would like to go back a little to what is going on. As a member of Parliament from an opposition party, I have had a chance to watch the implementation of the Tory agenda. At times I have been at a loss to explain what the government is trying to accomplish.
During the past four months, the government has introduced the UI bill which will place the entire burden on working Canadians and small businesses. We have also seen cuts to regional development funding to econmically depressed areas of Canada. We have seen the government support the Bank of Canada's high interest rate policies which again hurts small business and working people, while at the same time making Canadian exports more expensive. Now we have the goods and services tax which takes income out of the hands of Canadians and increases the cost of goods and services to consumers and the operating cost to small business.
When the election was in full swing, there were some comments made by the Minister of Finance, who at that time called the Leader of the Liberal Party and the Leader of the New Democratic Party liars, and I would like to refer back to that if I may.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: The Prime Minister never said that.

I said the Minister of Finance. In The Globe and Mail of October 31, he was quoted as saying, "Programs which are generally available such as medicare, pensions, old age security, aren't trade-distorting subsidies, and are not subject to trade laws".
The Leader of the Liberal Party in the debate Tuesday night said that he, the Prime Minister, has agreed to let the Americans have a say in the future of our social programs such as unemployment insurance and medicare. The Minister of Finance said, "I say to Mr. Turner, that is a lie". That is a quote from The Globe and Mail.
The comment was made by the Leader of the Liberal Party that our unemployment insurance programs were in jeopardy. The government has backed out of that

November 20, 1989
Government Orders
program and has now put it solely in the hands of the workers and the employers. The government does not contribute five cents so there is no subsidy and the Tories can say to their American friends that they are fulfilling our free trade agreement.
The New Democratic Party Leader said in the House of Commons that senior citizens want health and social programs maintained and enhanced for future generations. The trade agreement jeopardizes these programs, threatens to cut them as those in the United States, and the Minister of Finance said that is a lie too.
Here we have a piece of legislation that is going to for them over the years and are entitled to them. I want to say it is a sad day for me as the member of Parliament for Kootenay East to have to stand up here in this House and say to pensioners that this is what the government is doing to you.
I want to ask this question on behalf of the seniors in my riding who have come to me and asked what has this government got against the senior citizens. In the last Parliament the Tories brought in a drug patent law that changed the patent laws for drug distribution in Canada, and it has increased the cost of prescription drugs drastically. They tried to deindex old age pensions and through a strong fight by seniors' associations, we were able to stop them. Now they want to claw back our pension rights.
Another thing that they have done with regard to pensioners, and this has never been addressed, and it is another outright steal, is the changes to VIA Rail policy. Many of those seniors worked for the railways throughout the years, some 40 to 50 years service and have a pass on the railway. This government is going to take that away and those people who have paid for those passes through their working agreements are not even going to be able to travel on those trains.
What have you got against our seniors? That is what they are asking. I am proud to be a New Democrat and to look back at the history of Tommy Douglas and Stanley Knowles and many other people who have stood in this House, yes in opposition, and yes fighting for social democracy to bring about the kind of universal programs such as medicare, adequate pensions and universal
education programs. I think it is a sad day when we have to stand in this House and see our universal programs being tom away and deteriorated to this extent.
I say to the Conservative government, think about what you are doing. Listen to what the public is saying. Seniors are fed up, business people are fed up with your goods and services tax, the Chambers of Commerce are fed up. Every group across Canada is saying to you, "Listen to what we are saying because we are fed up. We are fed up with the tax grabs. We are fed up with what is going on and we want some people to start to listen to what we are saying and watch what we are doing".
I want to say that in any riding in British Columbia and in the neighbouring ridings in Alberta, the goods and services tax is one of the biggest items that the people are complaining about. It is a tax grab of the worst kind. When you start taking back from seniors and from young children through their family allowances-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Seniors making $50,000 a year.

The member who is from a riding in Winnipeg speaks of seniors with an income of $50,000. When you pay for something, you expect a return. When those people paid into those pension programs over the years, they expected a pension and if we want to look at a fair and equitable way, let us look at a fair taxation policy, a progressive taxation policy that will bring about some fairness.
The government has let us down. Whether it be pensions, drug prices, prescriptions, post-secondary education, whatever the programs are, the Conservative government has let us down. It cannot be trusted by the Canadian people and we as opposition members have to fight to let the public know exactly what is going on to ensure that we can keep these universal programs, and let us keep some social democracy in this country so that when the people are saying no to something, the government will start to listen.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: You don't represent the people. If you did, you would be in government and not in opposition.

We have a debate going on. I must have hit a nerve over there. Or maybe some of the members are beginning to realize that they have a responsibility to the seniors and to the family allowance recipients in their

ridings who are saying that they want to retain these universal programs.
When the Minister of Finance calls the leaders of the opposition parties liars during an election campaign when they tried to bring out our concerns, I object to that. I object very strongly to it. I do not think there is room in our society for that kind of comment or that kind of remark.
I do not want to speak too much longer, but I do want to say on behalf of our seniors, for goodness sake, roll it back, turn it back, vote against this legislation, give our seniors what is rightfully theirs and do not claw back their pensions.
